<meta>This page acts as an introductory disclaimer and usage guide for a book digitized by Google. It explains the transition of physical library volumes into the digital public domain.</meta>

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the <term>copyright</term> <note>Legal rights that grant the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution, usually for a limited time.</note> to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term> <note>Works whose intellectual property rights have expired or been forfeited, meaning they are now owned by the public rather than an individual creator.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia <note>original: "marginalia"; refers to the scribbles, comments, or marks made by previous readers in the margins of a book.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition</term> <note>Often abbreviated as OCR; the electronic conversion of images of typed, handwritten, or printed text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google "watermark" you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google's mission is to organize the world's information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world's books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at <insert>http://books.google.com/</insert>

# PREFACE TO THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

This Gospel is written according to Matthew; for Matthew himself, a disciple of the Lord, wrote this Gospel. At the beginning, he relates to us the birth of the Savior according to the flesh from the lineage of David. For this reason, he collects the genealogy until Christ, totaling forty-two generations. He presents in order the baptism by John, the temptation on the mountain <note>Original: "i lerinn." While "mountain" is the literal translation, it refers to the wilderness temptation.</note>, and the great signs and miracles performed by the Savior. He describes the choosing of the disciples, the mystery of the betrayal, and the end—how He was delivered to Pilate, was crucified in the body, and the body was placed in a tomb, and how the soldiers divided His garments. Likewise, he tells of the resurrection after two days <note>In the Armenian tradition, this refers to the "third day" (counting the day of the crucifixion as the first).</note> and the command given to the disciples to make disciples of all the nations and to baptize them. He commanded to be with them all the days until the end of the world.

Matthew wrote his Gospel in the city of Jerusalem in the Hebrew language <note>Early Christian tradition often held that Matthew originally wrote in Hebrew or Aramaic before the Greek version was produced.</note>, eight years after the Savior's ascension, at the request of the Church of Jerusalem. It contains 355 chapters <note>Original: "ՅԾԵ." These refer to the ancient "Ammonian" sections rather than modern chapters.</note>, 32 testimonies, and 2,600 verses.

->Matthew is translated as: The Exit of Life <note>Original: "Elk’ kenats." This is a traditional medieval Armenian etymological interpretation of the name.</note><-

---

*   In the original manuscript, the chapter headings of these Gospels were written inconsistently according to their source. For Matthew, it was written as: *The Beginning of the chapters of Matthew’s Gospel*; and for John: *The 8 Chapters of John’s Gospel*; while for Mark and Luke: *The Beginning of the chapters of the Gospel according to Mark*, or *Luke*. Looking at other more accurate examples, we have set them uniformly as is appropriate.
*   In the totaling of the harmonies <note>Refers to the "Canon Tables" or "Concordance" system used to find parallel passages across the four Gospels.</note>, as well as in the beginnings of chapters and their headings, many differences were found between various copies. Considering it unnecessary to note them here one by one, we have corrected the obvious errors in our copy according to the proper order.

<note>
**Vocabulary Notes:**
GOSPEL (Awetaran): Literally "Good News."
HEROD: Herod the Great, the Roman-appointed King of Judea.
EGYPT: Historically a place of refuge for Israelites during times of persecution.
BETHLEHEM: The city of David, where the Messiah was prophesied to be born.
JEREMIAH: One of the major prophets of the Old Testament.
NAZARETH: A town in Galilee; the term "Nazarene" became a common descriptor for Jesus and his followers.
JOHN THE BAPTIST: The forerunner of Jesus, practicing a baptism of repentance.
REPENTANCE (Apashkharut'iwn): A turning away from sin; a central theme in John's preaching.
</note>

"Woe to you, <term>Chorazin: a town in Galilee where Jesus preached</term>! Woe to you, <term>Bethsaida: a fishing village on the Sea of Galilee</term>! <margin>4 b</margin> At 그at time, Jesus went through the grainfields on the <term>Sabbath: the Jewish day of rest</term>. **Gospel:** The record of the life and teachings of Jesus.
**Parable:** A simple story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson.
**Sower:** A person who plants seeds by scattering them.
**Kingdom of Heaven:** A core theme in Matthew referring to God's reign.
**Weeds (Tares):** A plant that grows among grain; specifically darnel in this context.
**Prophecy:** A message inspired by God.
**Isaiah:** A major Hebrew prophet whose writings are frequently cited in the New Testament.

# PREFACE TO THE
# GOSPEL OF MARK.

The Gospel according to Mark was written by this same Mark, who was a disciple of Peter and a companion of Paul. He wrote this Gospel, setting the beginning by saying: "The beginning of the Gospel," starting from the preaching of John and the baptism of John. He draws testimony from the prophet Isaiah. He also indicates the temptation in the mountains, though he does not name the tempter <note>This refers to Mark 1:13, where the devil is mentioned but not described in detail as in Matthew or Luke.</note>. He recounts the selection of the disciples, and the signs and wonders which [the Lord] performed, as well as the mystery of the Incarnation <note>original: մարմնութեանն (marmnut’eann) – literally "the becoming flesh."</note> and the completion of His ministry. He tells of how He was delivered to Pilate and was crucified in the flesh; how the soldiers divided His garments; how His body was placed in a tomb and rose on the third day; and of the descent of the angel, the appearance to the women, and the command to tell the disciples.

By the command of Peter "the Rock," Mark wrote his Gospel in the city of Alexandria in the language of the Egyptians <note>While the Gospel was written in Greek, early Armenian traditions often associated its composition with Mark's mission to Egypt.</note>, twelve years after the ascension of the Savior. It contains 136 chapters, and 150 testimonies <note>Testimonies refers to Old Testament quotations or citations used within the text.</note>.

->Verses: 1070<-

Mark [means]: high, honorable, or "one who is above the roofs" <note>This is a traditional medieval etymology for the name Markos (Mark).</note>.

**Technical Vocabulary:**
* **Gospel (Աւետարան):** Literally "Good News." 
* **Mark (Մարկոս):** The traditionally attributed author of this Gospel.
* **Jesus Christ (Յիսուս Քրիստոս):** The central figure of the text.
* **John the Baptist (Յովհաննէս Մկրտիչ):** The forerunner who baptizes Jesus.
* **Baptism (մկրտութիւն):** A ritual washing; the Armenian term implies "immersion" or "washing."
* **Repentance (ապաշխարութիւն):** A change of heart or mind; also associated with penance.
* **Jordan (Յորդանան):** The river where John performed baptisms.
* **The Holy Spirit (Հոգին Սուրբ):** The third person of the Trinity, appearing here as a dove.
* **Satan (սատանայ):** The adversary or tempter in the wilderness.

# GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

<sig>A-G</sig>

CH. 16. (1) Some [read]: "They shall come and anoint." (2) Many manuscripts (+): "On the first day of the week." (3) Some: "Who will roll [it] away?" (4) Some: "The stone had been rolled away." (7) Some: "To <term>his</term> <note>original: "նր" (his)</note> disciples." (8) Some of the most ancient copies clearly end the Gospel of Mark here, placing the conclusion: "The Gospel according to Mark is finished," at this point. Such copies entirely omit the subsequent verses beginning with: "Jesus having risen," etc. <note>This refers to the famous "Short Ending" of Mark, where the original text may have ended at verse 8.</note> However, our copy, in agreement with many others, has printed the final mark: "Gospel according to Mark," and then provides a newly arranged heading for the following section, as if an addition: "Gospel according to Mark." Thus it begins: "Jesus having risen," etc. With which we also have compared and placed it in that manner. Where some follow only the Latin version, they continue these verses with the preceding text without any separation.

### Gospel according to Mark

* Having risen, Jesus <note>original: "յս", abbreviation for "Յիսուս"</note>, early on the first day of the week <margin>9</margin>, appeared to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. * And she went and told <margin>10</margin> those who had been with him, while they were mourning and weeping. * When they heard that he was alive and <margin>11</margin> had appeared to her, they did not believe. * Afterward, he appeared in <margin>12</margin> another form to those who were walking into the countryside. * And they went and told the others, and they did not believe them either. <margin>13</margin> * Later, while the eleven were reclining, he appeared <margin>14</margin> to them, and he rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen him risen from the dead. * And he said to them, "Go into all the world, and preach the gospel to all creatures. * He who <margin>15</margin> believes and is baptized shall live <note>meaning "shall be saved"</note>, and he who does not believe <margin>16</margin> shall be condemned. * Signs for those who believe <margin>17</margin> shall follow these things: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak in [new] tongues. * With their hands they shall pick up snakes; and if they drink any deadly poison <note>original: "դեղ", which can mean medicine, potion, or poison</note>, it shall not hurt <margin>18</margin> them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be healed." * And the Lord Jesus himself, after speaking with them, was taken up into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father. * And they, having gone forth, <margin>19</margin> preached throughout the whole earth, with the Lord's cooperation <note>original: "տն գործակցութբ", an abbreviation for "Տեառն գործակցութեամբ"</note>; and they <margin>20</margin> confirmed the word with all the signs that followed them.

# PREFACE TO THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

This is the Gospel written according to Luke. This same Luke was a disciple of Peter and was ordained as a companion to Paul, and was commended by him. He wrote this Gospel. He begins with the birth of John [the Baptist] and the events surrounding him. He also narrates the incarnation of the Savior; then, starting from there, he traces the lineage from Joseph to David, and back until Adam <note>Unlike Matthew, who traces the genealogy forward from Abraham to Jesus, Luke traces it backward to Adam to emphasize Jesus's connection to all of humanity</note>. He narrates the baptism of John, the temptation by Satan in the mountains, and the choosing of the disciples and the seventy others as well. 

He showed the signs and wonders performed by the Word made flesh <note>original: "Բնին", referring to the Divine Nature or the Logos</note>, the mystery of the betrayal, and the conclusion: how he was handed over to Pontius Pilate and was crucified in the body; how the soldiers divided his garments; and how one of the two thieves who were crucified with him repented through his confession. He also relates how his body was placed in a tomb and rose on the third day, and after this, he ascended into heaven while the angels looked on.

Luke, being a physician by trade, became a disciple of the Savior and was counted among the number of the Seventy <note>The "Seventy" (or Seventy-two) refers to the larger group of disciples sent out by Jesus in Luke 10</note>. Later, he became a disciple of Paul; for this reason, it is said that his "praise is in the gospel" <note>A traditional interpretation of 2 Corinthians 8:18, where Paul mentions a brother "whose praise is in the gospel"</note>. By the command of Paul, he wrote his Gospel in the city of Antioch in the Syriac language <note>While scholars today agree the Gospel was written in Greek, this text reflects an ancient tradition attributing a Syriac or Aramaic origin to the text for a local audience</note>, fifteen years after the ascension of Christ. 

It contains 148 <term>Kephalaia</term> <note>Ancient chapter-like divisions used for navigation</note>, 17 testimonies, and the same number of houses.
Luke: The Resurrection.

<summary>This page concludes the Gospel's table of contents and provides a historical preface identifying Luke as a physician and disciple of the Apostles who wrote his account 15 years after the Ascension.</summary>

<note>Glossary of technical terms from the source:
**Luke (Ղուկաս):** The author of this Gospel.
**Vinedresser/Laborer (մշակ):** A tenant farmer who works the land in exchange for a share of the harvest.
**Vineyard (այգի):** In biblical parables, often symbolizes the nation of Israel.
**Heir (ժառանգ):** The one intended to receive the property or legacy.
**Cornerstone (վէմ):** Literally 'rock' or 'stone'; the essential structural stone that holds a building together.
**Scribe (դպիր):** A scholar and teacher of the Jewish Law.
**Chief Priest (քահանայապետ):** High-ranking religious leaders in the Jerusalem Temple.
**Parable (առակ):** A simple story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson.</note>

### PREFACE TO THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

The Gospel of John was written by John, who is the brother of James, the son of Zebedee; he who reclined upon the Lord’s chest <note>A reference to John 13:23, identifying the author as the "Beloved Disciple"</note>—this same man wrote this Gospel. This work begins with the Eternal Word <note>original: "Ban," translating the Greek "Logos"</note> and records the birth according to the flesh by saying, "And the Word became flesh." This [Gospel] records the baptism of John and the choosing of the disciples, as well as the signs and wonders which he performed. It also records the end: how he was delivered to **Pontius Pilate**, the governor of Pontus, and was crucified; in which also the soldiers divided his garments and cast lots for his tunic; and his holy body was placed in a tomb. And he rose on the third day and appeared to his disciples himself.

John, who is also called the "Son of Thunder" <note>A title given to James and John by Jesus (Mark 3:17)</note>, recounted the final things to us with a voice like thunder. He wrote his Gospel thirteen years after the Savior’s ascension in the city of **Ephesus**, at the request of the Church of **Asia**, in the **Greek** language. And there are 332 chapters; 90 testimonies; 1,249 verses. Altogether, for the Four Gospels, there are 1,289 chapters; 79 testimonies; 6,056 verses.

John [means] obedience. <note>This is a traditional etymological gloss common in medieval manuscripts, though modern linguistics links the name to the Hebrew "Yehochanan," meaning "Yahweh is gracious."</note>

# PREFACE TO THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal divider consisting of a complex, repeating knotwork and floral pattern, flanked by small circular ornaments.</image-desc>

Those who once and for all desire the true and essential immortality—which brings one near to God <note>original: "atsamerdz" — a term meaning to be in close proximity or communion with the Divine</note> and makes one a lover of God—and who are the ministers of that heavenly and God-given virtue: they have established a noble goal for themselves. Foremost among these is that God-sprung blessedness of David <note>A reference to the Psalms of King David</note>, which is the rumination <note>original: "orochumn" — literally "chewing the cud," a common metaphor in early Christian writing for slow, meditative reading and digestion of the Scriptures</note> upon divine words, treasuring them day and night. For they are filled with joy through the inexhaustible and blessed truths of these meditations. Those who have devoted themselves to this, and have fallen in love with it, have tasted the fruit of this same divine mystery. They have gathered their minds from all wandering thoughts and henceforth look upward with focused intent toward that very immortality.

And now, for those who give such commands, it is right to obey and to be their servant at all times for their benefit. For it is a law for us—who have benefited from others—to always be useful to those in need, and to flee in due time from the condemnation of "envy" which is mentioned in the Gospel. 

First, I say that I have read and written the apostolic books in ten measures <note>original: "sturatun" — likely referring to stichoi, a method of measuring the length of ancient texts by line counts</note>. I previously sent these to a certain father among our brethren in Christ <note>The text uses the abbreviation "k'i" for Christ</note>, having labored with my meager and raw abilities. I was like an untrained young colt passing through a desert on an untrodden path, entering into the prescribed disciplines. For I did not find any among those who have been messengers of the divine word until this day who—to my knowledge—had taken such care regarding these specific books to show the results of their labor. 

+Not that I was so bold or arrogant as to take the labors of others and, without mercy, criticize them through the weakness of my limited knowledge regarding the selection of these readings. 

Now, as I said earlier and more recently: having read the books of Paul, and immediately following them these Acts of the Apostles, along with the Catholic Epistles <note><term>Catholic Epistles</term>: Also known as the General or Universal Epistles (James, Peter, John, Jude), so named because they were addressed to the church at large rather than specific congregations</note> of the Apostles, I have labored for an entire week and have now sent them to you. 

I beg you most earnestly not to be judgmental toward my twofold audacity and boldness. I pray that all the brothers and fathers, when they encounter this in due time, look upon it with love. Do not record my offenses and errors as a source of mockery, but rather correct them in a brotherly way, condescending to me for whatever may be found here. For the command of our fathers drew us to venture further than our ability allowed. 

And here, through the intimate care of our brothers, let us once again boldly set to work on things greater than ourselves in the Lord. 

+For love enters into the brothers and fathers at all times, and it shows no pride that contradicts itself within the body of the community. For there are laws regarding the Divine+, truly and rightfully brother-loving, which, by inclining us toward love, say clearly: "Love covers a multitude of sins" <note>A quotation from 1 Peter 4:8</note>. As for me, truly—

<meta>catchword: ra...</meta>

<summary>This page serves as a formal preface to the Acts of the Apostles and the General Epistles, where the translator expresses his humility and describes the spiritual importance of "ruminating" on scripture.</summary>
<keywords>Acts of the Apostles, Preface, David, Paul, Catholic Epistles, rumination, humility, biblical translation</keywords>

--- Page 268 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly preface to the Acts of the Apostles, focusing on the importance of constant meditation (rumination) on the Divine Word and the benefits of repetitive study.</meta>

...of the milk <note>original: "katoyn" — likely referring to the "spiritual milk" of basic Christian instruction mentioned in 1 Peter 2:2</note> and shall point it out more uprightly for those who examine it and for my friends. I shall narrate in detail the beautifully named and famous title: the namesake of divine oracles, the cultivation of wisdom, that constant **rumination** <note>original: "orochumn" — literally "chewing the cud," a metaphor for deep, repetitive meditation on scripture</note> which always increases in you, O Phasaq <note>A name or title, likely the patron or recipient of this manuscript</note>, who are surrounded by it as if by a hedge. You have acquired and gained its desirable name for yourself; through frequent and tireless repetition you have become practiced in it, and you remain established and full of blossoms. 

One of the **Platonists** <note>Refers to the followers of the Greek philosopher Plato; Armenian scholars often blended Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian theology</note> spoke the truth, guaranteeing us the most beautiful benefit from there, almost shouting it out, saying: "The repetition of a task is profitable." And he proclaims that the most wise, most good, and life-giving [God] considered all things to be a matter of practice. 

And now, if anyone has ever become sluggish in this, they remain indifferent to the profit of the path of blessedness, and by their own laziness, they become fruitless. The Psalm says: *Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.* <note>Psalm 1:1-2</note> For God desired all people to be without loss, mentally disciplined from above, and worshippers of God—to think upon and repeat all these thoughts, urging them forward through obedience to His commandments, saying: 

> Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength. And let these words which I command you today be in your heart and in your soul. And you shall instill them in your children, and you shall speak of them when you sit in your house, when you walk on the road, when you lie down, and when you rise up. <note>Deuteronomy 6:4-7</note>

And in this way, God desires us to be diligent, tireless and constant in this repetition. And so, taking boldness from the strict preservation of the divine command, the God-singing David said to God:

> Let the meditations of my heart be before you at all times, O Lord, my helper and my redeemer. <note>Psalm 19:14</note>

And now, this blessedness is for us an unerring and faultless reward for the practice of divine teaching. Conversely, for the one who is lazy in this, there is an unerring and unavoidable wretchedness from the divine side. Now, if there are some who are indifferent to this, they shall suffer that which the wretched shall suffer in the future. As it says: *Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law to do them.* <note>Galatians 3:10 / Deuteronomy 27:26</note> 

Therefore, one must never be sluggish or flee from the worship of God and the noble exercise of the mind’s laboratory. For it is graceful and conscious; it is more caring and productive, a mind that measures each benefit of its labors. For as much as one reaches the measure and knowledge of much learning, it encourages one to desire even more of the great and essential things. 

Just as someone among those who possess intellectual foresight finds a most noble art and, turning back even to the smallest details of it, examines and seeks it out—always stretching his own mind toward perfection by many **devices** <note>original: "mekenayiwk" — can refer to physical machines or mental "engines" and methods</note> and preparing himself even more—in the same way, may it happen to us through this profit-making, sweet-seeking reading. Day by day, in the assembly of the pious, let it train the soul through knowledge and make it wise.

<margin>+</margin>
Now, in what manner should lovers of reading be, and how should they constantly keep these things in mind? Especially we ourselves are debtors, and from close at hand, to keep in mind the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, along with the **Catholic Epistles** <note>original: "kat'oghikeayts'n" — also known as the General or Universal Epistles (James, Peter, John, Jude)</note>, to read them according to chapters and according to verses <note>original: "tants'n" — literally 'houses', a term often used in Armenian manuscripts for verses, stanzas, or poetic units</note>. And as much as it is necessary to choose the knowledge <term>gnosis (knowledge)</term> and the verses, and to distinguish the meanings from one another in small, minute parts, just as you commanded us, my dear brother **Athanasik** <note>A diminutive or affectionate form of the name Athanasius, likely the recipient of this work</note>. Regarding myself, I have acted without delay and with focused attention, arranging it verse by verse and entirely according to the foundation, according to my own weakness, in order to make the reading orderly. And I have sent to you, briefly and concisely, each according to its order, organized with a small number of verses in its entirety. First, concerning him who made the beginning of the Gospel account, who was from **Antioch** by race, a **physician** by profession, and a disciple of Paul; he wrote two books: the first being the Gospel, and the second the Acts of the Apostles. Now, all the words of these writings concern the Resurrection and the Ascension of Christ into heaven, and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles; and how the story is told by Christ's disciple, the Evangelist; and how many wonders occur through prayers and through faith in Him. [They also concern] the divine calling of Paul from heaven, his apostleship, and his wondrous preaching. But to say it all at once: it is about the endurance of the Apostles, which they bore for Christ's sake through many and great tribulations.

### Number of Chapters of the Acts of the Apostles:

<margin>+</margin>
Having received the pattern and the rule from the Fathers and the Teachers, we later put the Good News into practice through this focused arrangement of chapters. We pray that you do not blame our presumption—we who are limited by time and learning—in each verse that we shall read. Pray for us, that according to your prayers, grace may descend from above. Now, having found this testament <note>or 'document'</note> according to the cause of the scribe, assigning the chapters to him, and summarizing the individual parts, we shall mark the upper divisions near them. **Verses: 84** <note>Armenian numeral ձդ (84)</note>.

# CHAPTER 26

<margin>1</margin> Then Agrippa said to Paul: "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul, stretching out his hand, made his

<sig>ՆԱ</sig>

# PREFACE
## TO THE SEVEN
## CATHOLIC EPISTLES.

---

To venture a change in small things is not without hesitation. But I, the youngest, taking upon myself a labor beyond my measure—should I not be even more distressed? For example, if a small child thinks to cross the vast, encircling sea, and counts himself able to endure the stormy winds, yet when the waves move even a little, he cannot remain calm as the north wind begins to blow; rather, he finds himself in various troubles, and thus, tossed by the wind, the wretched child is placed in peril.

In the same way, I now know very well these anxieties of mine, which I undertake by my own audacity. But this is why I am willing: so that I may bring forth a worthy accounting. For the sake of submitting for all my sins—in which I also venture—I beseech you not to find any fault in me. But indeed, being compelled by the laws of love from you, my honorable brother <note>original: "եղբայր պատուական" — likely referring to the patron or a senior cleric who commissioned the work</note>, I have set myself to the task like a weak man among champions. Along with my labors, I always have hope for the reward of salvation. 

And truly, O my beloved leaders, do not be rejectors of my constant readiness; and bowing down in sympathy with these my present sorrows, with all your heart and with love, grant us the fruits of your prayers, bringing your pleas to God on our behalf. Let all the people of the church, gathered together with the ranks of the holy ones, offer unceasing prayers for us and be our intercessors. I know they will be benefactors after the example of those who once broke through the roof of the house and lowered the paralytic to Jesus; by their own faith, the one tormented by involuntary pains gained healing <note>A reference to the Gospel account in Mark 2:1–12 or Luke 5:17–26.</note>. 

Accept, therefore—accept from us with pleasure—this fruit, you merchant <note>original: "վաճառական" — a metaphor for the spiritual seeker or the recipient of the text</note> who invites us. Pray for us, that through our obedience we may be able to reach the goal. Now, I shall read these Catholic <note>The "Catholic" (Universal) Epistles include James, 1 & 2 Peter, 1, 2, & 3 John, and Jude.</note> epistles in order, verse by verse, and I shall set forth their philosophy and their divine fulfillment according to my weakness.

<summary>A humble preface to the Seven Catholic Epistles where the scribe compares his daunting task to a child attempting to cross a stormy sea and asks for the reader's prayers.</summary>

# PREFACE
## Of the Catholic Epistle of James.

James himself wrote to those of the twelve tribes <note>This refers to the "Twelve Tribes of the Dispersion," meaning Jewish Christians living outside of Israel</note> who had believed in our Lord Jesus Christ. He writes this instructional letter and teaches regarding various trials—explaining that temptation does not come from God, but from the hearts of men themselves. He teaches that it is right to show one's faith not by words alone, but through deeds; for it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous, but the doers of the law. Regarding the wealthy, he commands that they should not be honored above the poor in the churches, and especially that they should not be found to be prideful. Toward the end, he comforts those who have been wronged and commands them to be long-suffering until the coming of the Judge. He teaches about patience through the example of Job, making the virtue of patience appear desirable. He commands to call for the elders <note>The term "Elders" here refers to the priests or leaders of the early church community</note> for those who have fallen ill, and to hasten to bring back those who have strayed from the truth, so that one may receive a reward from the Lord and the atonement of sins. And thus he completes the letter.

## Chapters of the Epistle of James.

**1.** Concerning patience and unwavering faith, and concerning the humility of the rich. **1.** <note>The numbering here follows an ancient system of section markers rather than modern chapter numbers</note> In which he speaks of the fire within us, and that the troubles arising from it are not caused by God—rather, whatever is good within us is from Him.
**2.** Concerning gentleness, holiness, good works, giving glory through blessings, and concerning speaking with humility and restraint.
**3.** Concerning having love for each person without partiality <note>original: "առանց ակնառութե" — without "respect of persons" or favoritism</note>, according to the law.
**4.** That a person is justified not by faith alone, but also by works, and not without one of them.
**5.** That a reckless and undisciplined tongue kills its owner, which ought to be restrained for the glory and praise of God. **1.** In which he speaks of good conduct, and living without strife among one another, in contrast to the ambition of human wisdom. **2.** Concerning divine wisdom.
**6.** That through laziness and desire for pleasure, opposition and turmoil of deceit against God occur. **4.** <note>The Armenian numbering skips or follows a specific liturgical order here</note> Concerning repentance for salvation, and concerning not slandering one's neighbor.
**7.** That it is not by man's will but by God that all things proceed. **1.** In which he speaks of the greed of the rich and their worldly luxuries, and concerning the righteous judgment of God. **2.** Concerning long-suffering and patience in suffering, and concerning truth. **3.** Private instruction, and the reasons for each person's love through faith. **4.** That one must be a servant to one's neighbor in Christ.

James <note>original: "Յակոբոս Բառնա" — likely "The Discourse of James"</note> was written in Jerusalem <note>original: "յեմն" — abbreviation for Jerusalem</note> to the Hebrews in the Diaspora.

# THE EPISTLE

...for we all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man, able to bridle his whole body as well. <margin>3</margin> * See, we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, and we guide their whole body. <margin>4</margin> * Behold also the ships: though they are so large and are driven by fierce winds, they are guided by a very small rudder <note>original: "p'ok'r t'evovk'," literally "small wings" or "small fins," a Classical Armenian metaphor for a rudder</note> wherever the pilot’s will intends. <margin>5</margin> * So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. <meta>This page serves as the introduction and chapter index for the First Epistle of Peter. It follows the conclusion of the Epistle of James from the previous page, shifting focus from James’s practical exhortations to Peter’s message of comfort and hope for the scattered early Christian communities.</meta>

# P R E F A C E
## To the First Epistle of Peter

Peter writes this comforting letter to those of the <term>Diaspora [sp’iur’s]</term> who were Jews and had become Christians; and he strengthens those from among the Jews who had believed. He relates and demonstrates beforehand how faith in Christ was foretold by the prophets and through them it was clarified that salvation would come through His blood. This was preached to all—both to them and to the Gentiles—a mystery which even the angels longed to look into. Then he counsels them to live as holy ones, worthy of the one who calls them. He commands them to honor what is pure and holy, and instructs both women and men to be like-minded. He also gives some brief advice regarding daily habits. He shows that through the Lord’s resurrection, a saving preaching took place even in <term>hell [dzhokhs]</term> <note>original: "dzhokhs" refers to the "harrowing of hell" or the place of the dead</note>, and that those who had previously fallen asleep shall rise and be judged in the flesh. They were born through the grace of the resurrection; and since the end of all things is near, everyone must be prepared, as if they are to <term>give an account [ban taloy]</term> <note>literally "to give a word"</note> to the Judge; and so he concludes the Letter.

## Chapters of the First Letter of Peter the Apostle

1. Concerning the investigation of the new birth and concerning patience in trials, and concerning the salvific faith foretold beforehand by the prophets.
2. Concerning the hope and holiness which we owe because of our adoption <note>as children of God</note>, through careful conduct.
3. Concerning living worthily of that adoption in Christ, for the benefit of those <term>outside [artak’nots’n]</term> <note>referring to non-Christians or the secular world</note> for the glory of God.
4. Concerning being subject to rulers, and brotherly love and godliness. 
    1. Wherein [he speaks] of the submission of servants, and patient endurance without malice for the sake of Christ. 
    2. Concerning the submission of women, and harmony with their husbands, for the salvation of souls—following the example of Sarah. 
    3. Concerning husbands [behaving rightly] toward their wives. 
    4. Concerning the gentleness, calm, and lack of malice of all, following the example of God’s love for humanity; and having a shared feeling for the sufferings of Christ's death.
5. Concerning the rewards for [turning from] evil deeds, and producing the fruits of righteousness in the spirit, according to various and diverse graces.
6. That through communion with Christ one must overcome natural needs, and with hope in Him, endure the <term>torments [llkanats’]</term> inflicted by others.
7. Instruction for the <term>elders [erits’ants’]</term> concerning the oversight of the flock. 
    1. Wherein [he speaks] of the general duty of all: each through humility achieving victory against the adversary <note>referring to the devil</note>.
8. Prayer for the completion of faith.

# PREFACE
## To the Second Epistle of Peter

Peter himself writes this letter once again to the believers. In doing so, he provides a reminder of his first [letter], for he knew that his <term>departure from the body [pʻopʻokhoumn 'i marmnoy]</term> <note>original: "pʻopʻokhoumn 'i marmnoy" — literally "change from the body," a common ecclesiastical euphemism for death, reflecting 2 Peter 1:14.</note> was near. He hastens to quickly remind everyone [of his teachings], for which reason they should hear this doctrine at the end of his life. 

First, he speaks concerning faith, demonstrating it through the various wonders of the prophets; he shows that the prophecy concerning <term>Christ [Kʻristos]</term> <note>original: "kʻristosi" — abbreviated in the manuscript as "քնի".</note> is not of human origin, but was spoken from <term>God [Astvats]</term> <note>original: "ay" — an abbreviation for "Astutsoy" (of God).</note>. Then, he commands them not to pay any mind to the deceivers who would bring about their destruction, just as happened to the angels who sinned. 

He also explains in this letter that days are coming in which deceivers shall appear; they will wish to mislead some by saying that the promise of Christ's coming is in vain, mockingly claiming, "You always say he is coming, yet he does not come." He commands the faithful to especially flee from such people. He teaches them not to be short-sighted concerning the passage of time, for all time is considered as nothing before the <term>Lord [Tēr]</term> <note>original: "tn" — abbreviation for "tearn" (of the Lord).</note>; rather, one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years is as one day. He says only that you must be prepared for the Day of the Lord. 

He confirms this, demonstrates it, and commands everyone to be cautious, remaining in good works. He urges them to love what is written in the apostolic books and not to accept those who reject them, for such people despise all the divine scriptures. He reminds and teaches them to look forward to all the divine scriptures and to know the deeds of the past. Finally, he commands them not to fall from the firmness of their faith, and thus he completes the letter.

### Chapters of the Second Epistle of Peter

1. Concerning the calling through faith: establishing it with deeds of virtue toward the hope of future goodness.

2. A command to remember his teaching after his <term>passing [vakhchaneloyn]</term>; and how on the <term>mountain of the transfiguration [tʻapʻōr lerinn]</term> <note>original: "tʻapʻōr lerinn" — literally "the mountain of the procession," the traditional Armenian name for Mount Tabor, where Peter witnessed the Transfiguration.</note> he heard the voice of God concerning Christ.

3. A foretelling of the deception that shall come through heretics, their impiety, and their future torments.

4. A repetition of the evil deeds of heretical men.

5. Concerning how the Lord is to come suddenly at the end of this world; and the need to be found prepared with every virtue.

# THE EPISTLE
# OF PETER THE SECOND

## CHAPTER 1

1 **SIMON PETER, A SERVANT** <margin>4 2</margin> <note>This marginal note likely refers to a cross-reference or a liturgical reading cycle.</note>

# PROLOGUE
## To the First Epistle of John.

Since John, who wrote the Gospel, also wrote these <term>words [tars]</term> <note>original: "tars" — literally "letters" or "characters," referring here to the written scripture.</note> as a memorial for those who have believed in the Lord. And just as he did previously in the Gospel, so too in this epistle he <term>theologizes [adsabanē]</term> <note>original: "adsabanē" — to speak of the divine nature; in the early church, John was specifically known as "The Theologian" because of his focus on the divinity of the Word.</note> concerning the Word, showing Him to be always with the Father. In this writing, he calls the Father "Light," so that we might understand the Word also to be the Light of glory proceeding from Him. He theologizes and recounts that the <term>mystery [khorhurds]</term> <note>original: "khorhurds" — referring to the divine plan of salvation or the "hidden" reality of God's work.</note> revealed to us is not new, but has existed from the beginning and for all time. And now the Lord has appeared, who is eternal life and true God. He explains the reason for His coming and His appearance, saying that this occurred for the sake of destroying the works of the devil and liberating us from death; so that we may know the Father and His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

He writes to every age—to children, to youths, and to elders—that God has been made known; and henceforth the devil’s influence is defeated through the abolishing of death. Then, throughout the entire epistle, he teaches concerning love, desiring us to love one another; and he demonstrates that loving one another is good because Christ also loved us. He speaks concerning different kinds of fear and love, and about the children of God and the children of the devil. He also writes regarding sins that lead to death, and those that do not. He distinguishes between the different types of spirits, identifying which spirit is from God and which is from error, and teaches when we are recognized as children of God and when as children of the devil. He notes for which sins we ought to offer prayers for the sinner, and for which it is not appropriate to pray. Furthermore, he teaches that whoever does not love his neighbor is not of the Lord’s calling and cannot claim to belong to Christ. 

He also demonstrates the unity of the Son with the Father, and that whoever denies the Son does not possess the Father. He recounts in this letter the ultimate consequence: that whoever says Jesus Christ is not the Son of God is clearly shown to be a complete liar. He exhorts through this letter that those who believe in the Lord should not be sorrowful, nor should they be troubled by the hatred of the world, but should rather rejoice. For the hatred of this world proves that the believers have departed from the world and henceforth belong to the Kingdom of Heaven. At the conclusion of the letter, he mentions again that the Son of God is eternal life and true God, and that we should glorify Him, wait for Him, and keep ourselves from idols.

### Chapters of the First Epistle of John.

1. Gospel-based theology concerning Christ.
1. In which he speaks regarding confession and the caution needed to avoid sinning; and how those who keep the commandments of God confirm their knowledge of Him.
2. Concerning love, without which existence is a state of impiety.
1. In which there is an exhortation regarding grace according to each stage of life.
2. Concerning the renunciation of the love of this world.

<margin>8</margin> <note>Note that verse 7 is omitted in the main text here, as is common in ancient Armenian manuscripts, and discussed in the notes below.</note> ✱ And there are three that testify: the spirit, and the water, and the blood; and the three are one.

---

(5) Some [read]: And who is it that overcomes the world... [except he who] believes that **Jesus** is the **Christ** and the Son of God. (6) Some [read]: And by the blood of **Christ Jesus**. ✱ The Spirit is truth.

However, not only in other places, but also here, having taken from the Latin manuscripts, the Armenian text was altered according to this example: "Those who testify are three and the truth." <margin>7</margin> ✱ For there are three who testify in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. <margin>8</margin> ✱ And there are three who testify on earth: spirit, water, and blood; and the three are one. <margin>9</margin> ✱ If [we receive the testimony] of men. 

But in nearly all our manuscript examples, both old and new, which we have in hand—leaving aside two others until I can formulate the canon—only one of the new ones, written in <term>Thrassionis</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific scriptorium or a Latinized location name like Transylvania where Armenian printing or copying occurred.</note> in the year 1654 (about ten years before the printing [of the first Armenian Bible] began), places the text like this: "For the Spirit is truth. These three are they who testify in heaven: Father, and the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one; and there are three who testify on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood. If [we receive the testimony] of men..." 

And although there was one other identical copy that had this word written similarly in the upper margins, it clearly appeared that the first reading was more original, and the latter was adapted little by little by a later scribe in that interval. Our scribes generally desired that whether it entered from the fullness of Holy Scripture or from outside the pure books, the canonical discourse among the oldest Armenian manuscripts—the "sovereign" text—should be the one we felt compelled to place here.

# INTRODUCTION
## To the Second Epistle of John

In this letter, he writes as an elder to the church of the Lord, and to her children. Now, the reason for this letter is this: he saw that the children were walking well in the faith, but he heard that deceptive teachers had come, saying that the coming of Christ was not in the flesh <note>This refers to Docetism, an early belief that Christ only "seemed" to have a physical body.</note>. He writes concerning that matter as an inquiry; and first, he offers a gift of grace. Then he teaches that the mystery revealed to us is not a new thing. He commands them again concerning love, and that they should shrink from the corrupt teachings of those people. From this point on, he teaches that it is a sign of the impenitent <note>or "antichrists"</note> that they do not acknowledge the coming in the flesh; he commands that such teachers should not be received into the house, nor should anyone give them a greeting. And in this manner, he completes the letter.

## Chapters of the Second Epistle of John:

**1.** From the beginning, concerning an upright life through the love of God, remaining unchanging upon the foundation of faith. **1.** When he himself speaks regarding the duty [of avoiding] heretics in matters of worship or greeting; for they are [separated] from God. **2.** The promise of his coming to them with the hope of joy.

# PROLOGUE
## To the Epistle of Jude the Apostle.

This epistle he writes to the believers; and this is the reason: for certain men came and were teaching shamelessly, which was a denial of the Lord. It became necessary to write because of this and to strengthen the brothers, and first to entreat them to labor and strive for the faith handed down to them. Then he rebukes and sets apart the deceivers, and commands not to have any fellowship with them. For a calling alone is not sufficient if we do not walk worthily of that calling; for he says that the people who first came out of Egypt by the Lord <term>Lord: "տբ" (teramb), an abbreviation for "by the Lord"</term>, and did not remain in faith, perished. And the angels who did not keep their proper order, He did not spare; and he tells us to shun the coming punishments. And as Michael the archangel did not tolerate the blasphemy of Satan, he teaches that their trials will be like those of the people of Sodom. And then he gives a command regarding natural customs, and to offer prayers so they remain firm in the faith of the Lord, wherewith he completes the epistle.

* At the end, some [add]: "Completion of all the Catholic Epistles." <note>The "Catholic" or "General" Epistles include James, Peter, John, and Jude.</note> And almost all manuscripts, along with our own version, place the work of Andreas of Cappadocia <note>Andreas of Caesarea, a 6th-century bishop whose commentary on Revelation was highly influential in the Armenian tradition.</note>, "All things," etc., here after the Epistle of Jude, which we have left to be arranged in the supplement of the book.

* In our example, although the Revelation of John was placed here after the Catholic Epistles and before Jude, it seemed more appropriate—in comparison with all our other manuscripts and even the Greek ones—to arrange it at the end of the entire New Testament.

YA. <note>This is a signature mark (ՅԱ) indicating the sequence of the gathered pages in the printed book or manuscript.</note>

# P R E F A C E
## O F   P A U L   T H E   A P O S T L E
->Placed at the beginning of this Book.<-

---

Marvelling at your love of learning and your diligence, O honorable father <note>The "honorable father" likely refers to the patron who commissioned the manuscript or a monastic superior.</note>, seeing you as steadfast and firm, I have ventured into the narrow and subtle fortress of history to write the appropriate preface in this volume. Indeed, it would be a task far greater than my own abilities—to speak of that which is hated by the disobedient, where the son who is punished by a just penalty becomes a disobedient son in his instruction, while the obedient one becomes like Abraham. Now, supporting me with your humble prayers in my service, and like a small soaring boat, lift me up by them toward the Lord; just as back then, when the great Moses spread out his hands, the defeat of Beliar's <note>original: "Բելիար" (Beliar). A common name for the devil or the personification of wickedness, referring here to the spiritual enemies of Israel.</note> army occurred. Because I have promised to join these words upon those who have gone before, I have steered the skiff of speech, breathing toward a safe and peaceful harbor. And now, beginning this discourse after the manner of a laborer—as it truly is—I have considered the history with great care.

Paul the Apostle was a Hebrew by race, from the land <note>original: "գեղէ" (geghē), literally 'village,' but used here to denote the territory or tribal land.</note> of Benjamin; a citizen by education, a faithful bearer of the sent message; instructed and trained according to the Laws of Moses. Along with these things, he dwelt among the Cilicians in the magnificent, famous, and prominent city of Tarsus. He used to persecute and drive out the Church of God <note>The word for "God" here appears as a theological abbreviation (*titlo*) in the original.</note>. For this reason, he was a willing participant and an accomplice in the murder of those who killed Stephen—the one who was torn and longed for [Christ]—and he kept the garments of them all separately, like a manifest lion, so that he might free the hands of all others for the killing. Appearing as a leader among the cross-bearers <note>original: "խաչվարարսն" (khach'vararsn). Likely referring to those carrying out the execution or opposing the Cross.</note>, he strove everywhere to extinguish the greatness of the messengers. Many and great were the things that happened through him against the Church; nor was he found to be lacking in that manifest error. Rather, he desired to be even greater in it, and he thought he was establishing some great righteousness.

As he himself confesses regarding those many things, and as Luke relates in his two books <note>Referring to the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles.</note>: not only from long ago, like many of the Jews, did he hate [the truth] and go out from hatred against the preaching of the truth, but he even further provoked the whole nation to anger. For when he found the administration [of the Church] shining brightly, and the word of truth blossoming and glorified through these events more than the Jewish teachings, he thought to destroy the greatness of their teaching. He turned all his diligence and readiness toward the love of carrying the cross <note>i.e., his zealous opposition to it</note> against the Church, so that he might reject everyone from the true teaching, or work some vengeance worthy of the faith which is in Christ. Now, having taken letters of commission from the high priests and from the elders who were there in Damascus, toward those...

...who were among the persecuting Jews, he went forth with a command; driven by a frenzied zeal, like a fierce and well-fed beast <note>original: "ընջուղս" (ənjughs). When the Lord perceived that a wicked error was at work—as if he [Saul] held his own will to be like a bright dawn—He appeared to the fierce oppressor and separated him from the others by the intensity of that same light which appeared. And he underwent such a transformation that he, who had devised such great harm against the church and thought to utterly destroy all who brought the message of grace <note>original: "աղայեղաբերսն" (aghayeghabersn), likely referring to the "salt-bearing" or "grace-bringing" disciples, from 'agh' (salt/grace).</note>, was suddenly and instantly prepared as one beloved and faithful. Furthermore, he went to a certain disciple, Ananias of Damascus. He became a confidant of the ineffable mysteries, a defender and an expert, and a fellow-combatant in the preaching. And as the new preaching was confirmed in him by God, he received a new name for his salvation.

Such a fitting transformation took place in the blessed man that even his name was changed: he who was **Saul** throughout the churches was now named **Paul**. And so, having cut off his former zeal for chief impiety, whenever it was necessary for him to be apart from the truth of the disciples, he was likewise a willing servant. Not only in deeds, but also through his previous words, he had obtained the truth of his teachings; and being strengthened from both sides, he steadfastly proclaimed the impiety of the Jews to their own faces.

After a short time, having turned away, he went to Jerusalem <note>original abbreviation: "յեմ" (yem) for "Յերուսաղէմ" (Jerusalem).</note> to see Peter. These two, holy and courageous, divided the entire world between them: the side of the Gentiles was taken as the portion of Paul, for the Jewish side had been assigned to Peter. Passing through many cities and many lands, they wrote that through the faith of Christ <note>original abbreviation: "քնի" (k'ni) for "Քրիստոսի" (Christ).</note>, even the regions of Illyricum <note>original: "լիւրիկային" (liurikayin), referring to the Roman province of Illyricum on the Balkan Peninsula.</note> would be filled with godliness.

And God <note>original abbreviation: "ած" (ats) for "Աստուած" (God).</note> willed to advance him even further, so that as he traveled among men, the Gospel might perhaps be preached to all the Gentiles. 

Eventually, he went up to Jerusalem to care for the saints who were there and to distribute provisions to the poor. As soon as he arrived there, a stir arose in the city, and the common people were incited, until all the Jews together were in an uproar. They considered him an intolerable and heavy calamity and brought accusations against him, for he had once been a leader and participant in their error. Then, they did not need to increase the time of their examination beyond their own nine years; for he did not write down his testimony, since he wrote nothing for a third time. He too reached the fullness of time. And as a beloved one, he received the narrative in intimacy; for as many disciples as believed and fulfilled the order with faith, having received the commandments into the structure of their souls, they became heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

->**The Martyrdom of the Apostle Paul**<-

In the ninth year of the Roman Emperor <note>Nero</note>, the holy teacher Paul gave his testimony <note>original: "վկայեաց" (vkayeats), meaning he bore witness through martyrdom</note>, his head being cut off by the sword. This was in the 306th year of the life-giving sufferings of Christ our God <note>This likely refers to a specific chronological era used by the scribe, perhaps the Seleucid era or a local reckoning</note>, in the city of Rome. It was on the fifth of the month of **Panemos** <note>A Macedonian month roughly corresponding to July</note>, which is called by the Romans in advance the third of the **Kalends of July** <note>A Roman dating method counting backwards from the first of the month</note>, which is the month of the Martyrs. In this month, the holy apostle was perfected through a good testimony, in the sixty-ninth year of our Savior Jesus Christ the Lord, in the time of **Vagarsh** <note>Vologases I, King of Armenia and Parthia, used here to synchronize Roman and Armenian history</note>. At this same time, from which they testified, the commandment appeared and was looked upon by the consul and the fervent consul of those who love, the two brother emperors, our own Augusti <note>likely referring to the joint rule of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, though the chronology here is merging different historical traditions</note>. In the ninth seal of Python... in the five-hundredth cycle of the temple, in the month of January on the day of **Mareri** <note>The 10th month of the ancient Armenian calendar</note>, which was the twenty-ninth day of the month. This too I have precisely marked: the time of Paul’s testimony.

---

But apart from these prefaces and the lists of chapters for the **Acts** and the **Epistles** of the Apostles, certain canons <note>rules or structured lists</note> were made, as well as the full collection of readings from them which they perform during the days of the Church. In the first part, in the shortened version, there are also more extensive special testimonies from the **Old Testament** in each book from the infinite number of sources where they are seen in the **Greek original**. Our Armenian copies, having only the prefaces of the Epistles, we commanded to set the canon accordingly and through it—considering it an incomplete and useless separation—and also the defense of the twofold division specifically defined in the Greek sections.

# P R E F A C E
## To the Epistle to the Romans

He <note>The Apostle Paul</note> delivered this from Corinth, at a time when he had not yet seen them <note>the Romans</note>, but had greatly desired to see them. He had previously received word of their faith, and wrote as if he had already seen them. After this, he indicates that many times he had desired to come to them but was unable. Then, with the authority of a teacher, he made a decree concerning the calling of the **Gentiles** <note>original: "հեթանոսաց" (het'anosats) – non-Jewish nations</note>; and how, although the old era lasted for a long time, it is now abolished. He explains that they were subject to the transgression of Adam, and that the shadow of the law has passed away. He recounted the calling of the Gentiles in its proper order, showing that all men had become sinners through the occurrence of the law; thus, he prepared the nature of everyone—freed from an evil-natured will—to recognize God.

But now, they have been freed by their own will, as was previously determined for the **Greeks** <note>original: "հելլենացիս" (hellenatsis), referring here to the Hellenistic or pagan world</note>. God revealed the knowledge of Himself to them through the works of this world and His eternal power—which is His **Word** <note>original: "Բանն" (Bann), equivalent to the Greek 'Logos'</note> by which He created everything. Yet, these people did not recognize Him through His creations—that He is their creator and that the things He did not create are unpleasing—but rather they even worshipped the creatures themselves. He rebukes them for not keeping the natural laws even more so than the Jews; instead, by transgressing those laws, they dishonored God. And so, having judged both the Jews and the Greeks together, he hastens to put the old ways to death, so to speak; he does this to show that all are equal. Having declared everyone to be debtors, he moves to plead for grace and freedom.

He speaks also to the Jews about their coming, noting that the calling had reached the Gentiles, but through the promise. **Circumcision** and the shadowy laws have ceased. For he says that **Abraham** was justified not by circumcision, but before he was circumcised; and only then was he named Abraham. For he was to become the father of many nations who would be his sons through faith while uncircumcised; it was only after his righteousness that he received the sign of circumcision in his flesh, so that it might be a sign for those who were to be his physical descendants. Circumcision was destined to cease once the Gentiles became the sons of Abraham. It is necessary to model ourselves after the faith of Abraham, by which he was justified while circumcision was not yet in him. 

He called this "grace" granted to Abraham, and through his words he addressed the sign, for the sign was to cease. If the Gentiles were forced to be circumcised, the name of "Abraham" <note>meaning 'Father of Multitudes'</note> would be hindered, and he would merely be called "Abram" <note>meaning 'Exalted Father'</note>, whereas he was renamed Abraham by God. He does not wish for the Gentiles to be circumcised, nor even those who were Jews in the flesh; for the name was never established by this rite, but rather he was called the father of many nations. Therefore, there is no need for them to be circumcised; the faith of Abraham is sufficient. We are justified not by anything from the shadowy laws, but by faith, just as Abraham was. All these things he imprinted in this way; and he shows again that no one else was ever a savior through grace to both Jews and Gentiles, erasing the first sins...

...of the nations <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "heathen nations"</note> which were among all people, they were unable to find a remedy by any other word. 

But Christ is all. For the curse which existed from the beginning was impossible for anyone else to remove, nor could anyone else provide salvation. Indeed, it would have been impossible for anyone else, had the Son of God not clothed Himself in the body and become man. He offered this for the sake of all, so that He might free everyone from death. Likewise, just as sin entered the world through one man <note>referring to Adam</note>, for this reason grace also came through one man <note>referring to Jesus Christ</note>. 

He <note>Paul</note> set himself to comfort the **Jews** <note>original: "հրէայսն" (hreaysn)</note>, so that they would never be called transgressors of the Law if they believed in Christ; and he sought to reconcile the **Gentiles** <note>original: "հեթանոսն" (het'anosn)</note> so that they would never be prideful over the Jews. Rather, they should know that they are branches grafted onto the root, for they themselves took root from them. After this, he completed the word of teaching for them regarding the righteous plantings.

# Chapters of the Epistle to the Romans

Concerning the Gospel teaching on the righteousness of the grace of Christ, and those who live under that grace; and concerning foresight and the wisdom of virtue.

1. First, after the beginning, regarding the condemnation of the Gentiles who did not keep the natural law.
2. Regarding the condemnation of the Jew who did not keep the written Law <note>The Mosaic Law</note>.
3. Regarding the advantage of the Jew, which was entrusted to them <note>The oracles of God</note>.
4. Regarding the grace by which alone men are justified—not according to the choice of the elder, but according to God the Giver—to be justified by faith, following the example of Abraham.
5. Regarding the hope of things to come.
6. Regarding the gift offered for the salvation of man through Jesus Christ, in exchange for the fall of the first earth-born, Adam.
7. Regarding the trial of good through precious faith.
8. Second—regarding the grace of life.
9. Regarding condemnation under the Law on account of sin.
10. Regarding the inability of human nature to fulfill the rational laws within us on its own.
11. Regarding those drawing near to the requirements of nature through union with the Spirit.
12. Second—regarding the glory of the saints to come.
13. Regarding the supernatural love of Christ toward us.
14. Regarding the fall of the Jew and their exile, and the calling of the truth which was granted to the Gentiles.
15. That according to their rebellion, exile came upon the class of those destined for destruction, as they were not prepared for the preaching.
16. Regarding the olive tree through which they <note>the Gentiles</note> were grafted, so that some might strive to enter a second time, joining the zeal of the Gentiles, and being ordered among those who believe in Christ.
17. Exhortations regarding the virtues toward God and toward men:
    a. In which was the grace of single-minded unity.
    b. Regarding the worship of God.
    c. Regarding being unimpeded in spiritual matters.
    d. Regarding following rulers; to be respectful toward them and to follow their lead.
    e. Regarding acting with a proper mind concerning foods.
    f. Regarding being imitators of the **Divine Economy** <note>original: "տնօրինականութեանն" (tnorinakanut'eann) — the way God manages the world and salvation</note>.
18. Regarding the good service performed in the East and in the West.

<margin>ԴԴ 1</margin> Do you not know, brethren (for I speak to those who know the law), that the <term>law</term><note>original: 'ōrēnk’'; referring here to the Mosaic Law or the general principle of law</note> has dominion over a man as long as he lives? ✱ For a woman who has a husband is bound by the law to her husband while he lives; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. ✱ So then, if while her husband lives, she belongs to another man, she is called an <term>adulteress</term><note>original: 'shun'; literally 'dog', but used here as the root for adultery</note>. 11. And know this regarding the time, that it is already the hour for us to wake from sleep; for now our salvation <note>original: "փրկութի", abbreviation for "փրկութիւն" (salvation)</note> is nearer to us than when we [first] believed. 
12. The night is far gone, and the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. 
13. Let us walk honorably as in the daytime, not in revelry and drunkenness, not in debauchery <note>original: "խառն ընկողնոք", literally 'mixed beds'</note> and impurity, not in quarreling and jealousy. 
14. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ <note>original: "յս քս", abbreviation for "Յիսուս Քրիստոս" (Jesus Christ)</note>, and make no provision for the flesh to fulfill its lusts.

->CHAPTER 14<-

1. Receive the one who is weak in faith, but not for the sake of doubtful disputes. 
2. One believes he may eat all things, but the one who is weak <note>original: "հիւանդն", literally 'sick' or 'infirm', used here for spiritual weakness</note> eats [only] vegetables. 
3. Let not the one who eats despise the one who does not eat, and let not the one who does not eat judge the one who eats; for God <note>original: "ած", abbreviation for "Աստուած" (God)</note> has received him. 
4. Who are you to judge another’s servant? To his own master <note>original: "տն", abbreviation for "տեառն" (master/Lord)</note> he stands or falls. But he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand. 
5. One person esteems one day over another, and another esteems every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. 
6. He who observes the day, observes it for the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, for the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats for the Lord, and gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, for the Lord he does not eat, and gives thanks to God. 
7. For none of us lives to himself, and no one dies to himself. 
8. For if we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

<note>The vocabulary list below clarifies technical terms used in the Armenian text.</note>
**TO THE ROMANS:** The title of the epistle.
**CHAPTER 15:** The chapter designation.
**strong/capable:** Refers to those with a mature conscience.
**edification:** The process of spiritual growth and building up the community.
**reproaches:** Insults or shaming directed at someone.
**patience:** Enduring perseverance.
**comfort:** Encouragement or consolation.
**glorify:** To give honor or praise.
**Gentiles:** Non-Jewish nations or peoples.
**Isaiah:** The Old Testament prophet quoted here.
**peace:** Spiritual tranquility.
**instruct:** To advise, warn, or teach.
**minister:** One who serves or performs a sacred office.
**shall hope:** The act of placing trust in a future promise.

# P R E F A C E
## To the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

He sent this from Ephesus of the Asians <note>original: "յեփեսոսէ ասիացւոց," referring to the Roman province of Asia Minor</note>; for he had seen that they were [influenced] by certain distinct teachers. He makes mention of this through this spirit, and for the sake of this spirit. The assembly of Corinth had been overcome by the Lord, and they were thinking of causing harm <note>original: "պատակփել," likely a corruption or variant of "պատակել," meaning to deceive or cause ruin</note>, and there was division among them. And from such a <term>schism</term> <note>original: "հերձուած," a formal split or faction within the church</note> it came to pass that one took his father’s wife. Others thought to separate from their wives under the pretext of religious practice. Some ate of the sacrifices to idols and frequented those meals. Others were ignorant of such things. And those who spoke in marvelous tongues thought they had reached the end [of spiritual perfection] and walked in this [belief]. And concerning the mystery of the resurrection, they said this body shall not rise. All these [issues] having been stirred up in Corinth, the assembly wrote to the Apostle; and he sent back this letter to them all. 

And first, he bears witness only to their wisdom and knowledge, yet he does not permit them to create such a schism. Rather, he counsels them not to shorten matters with words alone, but to show them through effort and power. And from here, he instructs the one who had taken the deep [sin] <note>Refers to the case of incest in 1 Cor 5</note>, as well as those who had no sin in themselves, and those about whom they wrote. He gives [instruction] on marriage; that teachers should be holy, as should marriage, and that it may be set aside for a time for the sake of prayer. And to those who loved <term>abstinence</term> <note>original: "ծուժկալութի," meaning self-control or asceticism</note>, he writes concerning virgins—yet not by compulsion, but because they became so through faith. And concerning the sacrifices to idols, [he writes] so that they might not defile their conscience, but rather conduct themselves with love. He causes those things involving sacrifices to cease, so that they might not be grieved in exchange. And to those who possessed spiritual gifts, he writes so that they might not be untried in those gifts, or condemn those who do not have such gifts; for those who are thus, he says all come from one and the same Spirit. He also demonstrates the teaching on the resurrection: that this body rises, a transformation of corruption occurs, and it rises without corruption according to the grace of Christ, the same who raised Christ and [will raise] us with Him. And at the conclusion, he writes words of praise to his own, and gives commands concerning the saints, and thus completes the letter.

---

->Chapters of the 1st Epistle to the Corinthians:<-

The contents which the letter holds regarding the corrections of the Corinthians' transgressions:
1. Regarding those who, from the beginning, were divided against each other in Christ due to the vanity of human wisdom. 2. Concerning divine wisdom. 3. Concerning the ministers. 4. Concerning not disparaging the teachers. 5. Concerning not being proud.
6. Concerning fornicators and fornication, and those who associate with them. 7. Concerning the judging of the righteous by external <note>meaning secular or pagan</note> judges, and that being before unbelievers. 8. In which also [is discussed] the matter of not rising <note>Refers to those doubting the resurrection</note>. 9. Concerning marriage and widowhood, and not marrying.

-># TO THE CORINTHIANS<-

# EPISTLE

<margin>16</margin> Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ <note>original: "քսի" (k’si); abbreviation for "Քրիստոսի" (K’ristosi), meaning "of Christ"</note> greet you. <margin>17</margin> I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and scandals contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and avoid them. <margin>18</margin> For such people do not serve our Lord <note>original: "տն" (tn); abbreviation for "Տեառն" (Tyarn), meaning "of the Lord"</note> Christ, but their own bellies; and by smooth talk and blessings <note>or flattery</note> they deceive the hearts of the innocent. <margin>19</margin> For your obedience has reached everyone, and now I rejoice in you; but I want you to be wise in what is good, and innocent in what is evil. <margin>20</margin> And the God <note>original: "ած" (ats); abbreviation for "Աստուած" (Astvats), meaning "God"</note> of peace shall crush Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <note>original: "յսի քսի" (ysi k’si); abbreviations for "Յիսուսի Քրիստոսի" (Yisusi K'ristosi)</note> be with you. <margin>21</margin> Timothy, my brother and fellow worker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen. <margin>22</margin> I, Tertius, who wrote this letter in the Lord, also greet you. <margin>23</margin> Gaius, my host and the host of the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the treasurer <term>shahap (շահապ): a term derived from Persian, used here for a city steward or treasurer</term> of this city, and Quartus the brother, greet you. <margin>24</margin> Now to Him who is able to establish you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery which was kept secret for long ages, <margin>25</margin> but now is made manifest through the prophetic writings, according to the command of the eternal God <note>original: "այ" (ay); abbreviation for "Աստուծոյ" (Astudzo), meaning "of God"</note>, for the obedience of faith among all nations, <margin>26</margin> to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to Him be glory forever and ever. Amen. <margin>27</margin> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
