# P R E F A C E
## To the First Epistle to the Corinthians

He <note>The Apostle Paul</note> sent this from Ephesus of the Asians, because he had seen those 
<margin>1.</margin> whom he had taught; he mentions this by his own hand and 
for his own reasons. The assembly of Corinth had been overcome by a loss of 
love, and they were thinking of tearing themselves apart, and there was division among them. And 
from such schisms <note>original: "հերձուածոյն" (hertsuatsoyn); refers to divisions or sects</note> they came forward to take the father's wife <note>A reference to the case of incest mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5:1</note>. Others 
thought to separate from their wives under the pretext of religious observance. Some 
were eating from the sacrifices of idols and were frequenting the [idolatrous] processions. Others 
disdained the vessels <note>likely referring to the communal vessels of the Lord's Supper</note>; and some spoke in miraculous tongues, thinking 
and moving toward the end in this way. And concerning the mystery of the resurrection, they 
said: "this body shall not rise." All of these people in Corinth being thus moved, 
 the assembly wrote to the Apostle, and he sent back this 
Epistle to all of them. And first, he only testifies to them regarding their wisdom 
and knowledge, and he does not [at first] venture to rebuke them for such schisms; but 
he consults with them—not to be religious only in words, but to 
show it through effort and power. And he rebukes him who had taken his stepmother <note>original: "զմօրուն" (zmōrun); literally 'the father's wife'</note>. He also gives instruction 
concerning those who did not take their sins upon themselves, and concerning those things about which they wrote. 
Regarding marriage, he teaches that marriage is holy, and 
at the proper time it may be suspended for the sake of prayer. And to those who 
loved self-control <note>or celibacy</note>, he writes concerning their promise; yet not by compulsion, but 
so that they might be so by faith. And concerning the sacrifices of idols, [he writes] so that they might not 
defile their conscience, but might conduct themselves with love. He 
causes that which comes from sacrifices to cease, so that they might not boast in their stead. 
<margin>2.</margin> And to those who were in possession of spiritual gifts, he writes so that they might not be arrogant 
<margin>3.</margin> in those gifts, or condemn those who do not perform such gifts; 
<margin>4.</margin> or those who are such, he says all are of one and the same Spirit. He 
shows through teaching also concerning the resurrection, that this body rises; it 
comes to an end in corruption, and rises without corruption according to the 
grace of Christ, and the same [Spirit] who raised Christ shall also raise us with him. And at 
the conclusion, he writes words of transition to his own affairs, and concerning the collection for the saints 
he gives commands, and thus he completes the Epistle.

### Chapters of the 1st Epistle to the Corinthians

The Epistle contains the various types of conduct and transgressions of the Corinthians:
1. After the beginnings, concerning not being in conflict with one another for the 
glory of human wisdom.
2. Wherein is concerning divine wisdom.
3. Concerning servants <note>ministers/deacons</note>.
4. Concerning not boasting in teachers.
5. Concerning not being proud.
6. Concerning fornicators and fornication, and those who would be their associates.
7. Concerning not snatching [justice] from righteous [judges] by going to external judges, and that 
even before unbelievers.
8. Wherein is also concerning not committing fornication.
9. Concerning marriage and widowhood, and not marrying.

Some, through being accustomed to idols until now, eat [the food] as if it were a sacrifice; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. * But food does <margin>8</margin> not bring us before God. If we do not eat, we lack nothing; and if we eat, we gain nothing. * But <margin>9</margin> take care lest this liberty <note>original: "իշխանութիդ" (ishkhanut'iwd) — literally "authority" or "power" to act</note> of yours becomes a stumbling block <note>original: "գայթաղկութի" (gayt'aghkut'iwn)</note> to the weak. * For if someone sees you— <margin>10</margin> you who have knowledge—reclining [at a meal] in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, being possessed by weakness, be "built up" <note>Paul uses the word "built up" (շինիցի) ironically here, suggesting the weak person is "encouraged" to do something they believe is wrong</note> to eat what is sacrificed to idols? * And so the weak <margin>11</margin> brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge. * And thus, by sinning against the brothers and <margin>12</margin> wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. * Therefore, if <margin>13</margin> food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble.

He concludes by beginning a defense of his own apostolic authority and freedom.</summary>

# FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS

2 Indeed, you are the work of my labor in the Lord. * Even if I am not an apostle to others, yet I certainly am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
3 My defense <note>original: "պատասխանի" (pataskhani) — a legal defense or formal reply</note> to those who would examine me is this:
4 Do we not have the authority <note>original: "իշխանութի" (ishkhanut'iwn) — meaning the right or power to act</note> to eat and to drink?
5 Do we not have the authority to take a sister-wife <note>original: "զքորս կանայս" (zk'ors kanays) — likely referring to a Christian woman/wife who travels in ministry</note> around with us, as do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas <note>The Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter</note>?
6 Or is it only I and Barnabas who have no authority to refrain from manual labor?
7 Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not eat of the milk from the flock?
8 Do I say these things merely by human [standards]? Or does the Law <note>The Jewish Torah</note> not say the same?
9 For it is written in the Law of Moses: "You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 25:4</note> Is it for oxen that God is concerned?
10 Does He not surely say it for our sake? Indeed, it was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes, in hope of enjoying [the harvest].
11 If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap material things <note>original: "զմարմնաւորսդ" (zmarmnaworsd) — literally "fleshly" or "physical" things, meaning financial support</note> from you?
12 If others enjoy this authority over you, do we not even more? But we have not made use of this authority; instead, we endure all things, so that we may not cause any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ.
13 Do you not know that those who perform temple duties eat from the temple, and those who serve at the altar enjoy a share of the altar?
14 In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who preach the Gospel should live by the Gospel.
15 But I have not used even one of these [rights]. And I have not written this so that it might be so [done] for me...

->FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS<-

* Since there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of that one bread. <margin>18</margin> * Consider Israel according to the flesh <note>original: "ըստ մարմնոյ" (ust marmnoy) — meaning the physical descendants of Israel</note>; are not those who eat of the sacrifices participants in the altar? <margin>19</margin> * What then am I saying? That what is sacrificed to an idol is anything? Or that an idol itself is anything? <margin>20</margin> * Rather, what the Gentiles <note>original: "հեթանոսք" (hetanosq) — heathens or pagans</note> sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons; for you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. <margin>21</margin> * And you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. <margin>22</margin> * Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He? <margin>23</margin> * Everything is permissible for me, but not everything is beneficial. Everything is permissible for me, but not everything builds up. <margin>24</margin> * Let no one seek his own [good] alone, but also that of his neighbor. <margin>25</margin> * Eat everything that is sold in the meat market, and do not ask questions for the sake of conscience. <margin>6</margin> <margin>26</margin> * For the earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it. <margin>27</margin> * If any of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat everything that is set before you, and do not ask questions for the sake of conscience. <margin>28</margin> * But if someone should say to you, "This was sacrificed [to an idol]," do not eat for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience. <margin>29</margin> * But I speak of conscience—not one's own, but the neighbor's. For why should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience? <margin>30</margin> * If I partake with grace <note>original: "շնորհօք" (shnorhoq) — thanks or grace</note>, why am I slandered for that which I give thanks? <margin>31</margin> * Therefore, whether you eat, or whether you drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. <margin>32</margin> * Be without offense <note>original: "առանց գայթագղութե" (arrants gaytagghutyan) — without causing a stumbling block</note> to Jews and to Gentiles and to the church of God. <margin>33</margin> * Just as I also please everyone in all things; I do not seek my own benefit, but that of the many, so that they may be saved.

## CHAPTER 13

1 **I**f I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not love, I have become like sounding brass or like clanging cymbals. 
2 * And if I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries <note>original: "խորհուրդս" (khorhurds) — can also mean secrets or sacraments</note> and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to move mountains, and have not love, I am nothing.
3 * And if I give away all my possessions to the poor, and if I deliver my body to be burned, and have not love, I gain nothing.
4 * Love is patient and kind; love does not envy, does not boast, and is not proud.
5 * It does not act unbecomingly, does not seek its own, is not provoked, and thinks no evil. 
6 * It does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices in the truth.
7 * It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.
8 * Love never fails; if there are prophecies, they shall be finished; if there are tongues, they shall cease; if there is knowledge, it shall be finished.
9 * For we know in part <note>original: "փոքր 'ի շատէ" (pokr 'i shate) — literally "a little from much," meaning partially</note>, and we prophesy in part.
10 * But when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be finished. 
11 * When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
12 * For now we see as through a mirror, dimly <note>original: "օրինակաւ" (orinakav) — by way of an example or riddle</note>, but then face to face; now I understand in part, but then I shall know even as I am known by Him.
13 * But now abide faith, hope, and love—these three—and the greatest of these is love.

<term>edification (շինութի)</term> A central theme in Paul’s writing, meaning to build up the spiritual strength of the community.
<term>Voskan (Ոսկան)</term> Refers to Oskan Yerevantsi, who edited and printed the first complete Armenian Bible in Amsterdam.
<term>unlearned (ագիտին)</term> From the root 'not-knowing'; refers to a person lacking specific knowledge or a lay member of the congregation.

<summary>This page contains 1 Corinthians 14:2-17, where the Apostle Paul argues that the gift of prophecy is superior to the gift of tongues because it provides clear edification for the entire church. He uses the analogies of musical instruments and bugle calls to emphasize the necessity of clear, intelligible communication in worship.</summary>

<term>Corinthians</term>: The inhabitants of Corinth to whom Paul wrote.
<term>Resurrection</term>: The rising from the dead into a new form of life.
<term>Body/Flesh</term>: The physical or "natural" vessel of human life.
<term>Spirit</term>: The eternal or "heavenly" aspect of the person.
<term>Corruption</term>: The state of being subject to decay and death.
<term>Immortality</term>: Eternal life that is no longer subject to death.
<term>Adam</term>: The biblical first man, used here as a prototype for humanity.

# P R E F A C E
## To the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

This letter was sent from Macedonia; and this is the reason for this letter: The Corinthians received the first letter and repented for the sins of the man who had committed an offense against his stepmother <note>original: "զմորուն" (zmorun) — referring to the case of incest described in 1 Corinthians 5:1</note>; and they were grieved when they recognized such sins; they removed the cause of division from among them. And those who stood by the letter of the law <note>The Judaizers or legalists who insisted on Mosaic law over the Gospel</note> terrified them by revealing the graces of Christ; and especially those who appeared like them <note>The "false apostles" who imitated Paul's authority</note> boasted before their eyes. Because of this, he [Paul] urges the holy faith well here, and he first accepts the one who had acted lawlessly among the good [the repentant man]; and after this, he deems him worthy through pleas and repentance, and gives the command to receive him. According to the same teacher, concerning the laws, one should not act according to the letter of the law alone; but through this writing, he reveals them; for the law is not in vain, but possesses the wisdom of the Holy Spirit. After this, by the coming of Christ, there became a new creation; and no one can exist according to the old, but in the new creation all are renewed, and cease from circumcision. He accepts [them] concerning the ministry, and first he proves and exhorts them to excel in this; and he shows himself as the cause for those who boast to the face; he says that all who were changed in the Lord saw the vision of revelations, and his being snatched up into paradise and into the third heaven. After this, he commands them not to sin but for the sinners to repent, and he completes the letter with thanksgiving.

## Chapters of the 2nd Epistle to the Corinthians:

These words of the letter concern himself [Paul], the Corinthians, and the false apostles. For these reasons, he proceeds to speak first about the graces of God and about good virtue, according to those with good minds and those who struggle, and about being incomprehensible; and about the ministry of the apostolate, and about the arrogance and wickedness of the false apostles.

**1.** Thanksgiving for God’s help, in which he exhorts them to be prepared.

**2.** Concerning his love for them and sparing them from grief, although by grieving them he worked for their benefit; as with that man whom he rebuked with punishment and then commanded to grant grace <note>original: "շնորհել" (shnorhel) — here meaning to forgive or show favor</note>.

**3.** Concerning his divine visits <note>original: "զստիցն" (zstits'n) — referring to his stays or presence among them</note> for necessary needs, concerning which he speaks while moving forward.

**4.** Concerning the ministry according to the Spirit, and the divine glory according to the law.

**5.** Concerning divine glory and the orderly life, so that he may be recognized by his fruits <note>literally "intestines" or "inner parts," here meaning inner character or fruits</note>.

**6.** Concerning the weakness of the flesh, and the stripping off of it and putting it on once again <note>An allusion to 2 Corinthians 5, comparing the body to a tent or garment</note>.

**7.** Concerning his divine discourse <note>original: "ածախրոսութե" (astvatsakhrosut'yun) — speaking about God or divine matters</note> and brotherly love according to Christ.

**8.** The acceptance of the Corinthians with obedience and love, which made him rejoice.

**9.** Encouraging the giving of gifts to the saints, and the punishment of those who—

# PREFACE
## To the Epistle to the Galatians.

He <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> sends this from Rome <note>Ancient traditions often assigned various locations for the writing of the epistles; most modern scholars believe Galatians was written earlier, likely from Ephesus or Antioch.</note> to those whom he had personally seen and taught. The reason for this letter is as follows: The citizens had been well-instructed by the apostle and were established in a close relationship with Christ <note>original: "քսի" (k'si), abbreviation for "Քրիստոսի" (K'ristosi)</note>; they were fellow-travelers with the apostle. However, they were enticed by certain people to be circumcised. Having heard all this from some people, the apostle writes to them. First, he bears witness to them regarding the faith they held in the intimate covenant of Christ <note>original: "քնի" (k'ni), abbreviation for "Քրիստոսի" (K'ristosi)</note>, and he reproaches them, saying they acted with foolishness, and he rebukes them. After this, he does not accept the Law <note>The Mosaic Law or Torah.</note> according to the faith of Abraham, and he demonstrates this from the Law and through the allegorical example of the wives of Abraham. He shows that circumcision was given for a specific time, and now it has ceased because of the coming of Christ. In this way, he showed that they should never transgress, but rather hold to the faith of Christ and know that the grace which is in Christ drives out the circumcision that is in the flesh. Thus, having expressed his message with his usual concluding praise, he finishes the Epistle.

### Chapters of the Epistle to the Galatians:

1. After the beginning, the account of his own turning from Judaism according to revelation.
2. Concerning the witness of the apostles that life comes from faith.
3. Concerning the opposition to Cephas <note>original: "Կեփայի" (Kep'ayi). This is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter, meaning "Rock."</note>, and that salvation is by faith and not by the Law.
4. That holiness is by faith and not from the Law.
5. That even Abraham was justified by faith, as an example for us.
6. That the Law does not justify, but convicts and places a curse upon one, which Christ dissolves.
7. That goodness comes from the promises, not from the Law; and the Law was previously a source of conviction.
8. That those under the Law were under the elements <note>referring to the "elements of the world" or basic principles.</note>.
9. Concerning the wives of Abraham and the son of the bondwoman <note>referring to Hagar and Sarah</note> as an example and instance: one must not serve the Law.
10. That our calling is not under circumcision and the Law, because of Christ's sufferings.
11. Establishment by Christ according to the freedom of the Spirit.
12. Turning away from those who boast in circumcision, and the willingness for new life in the Spirit.

# PREFACE
## To the Epistle to the Ephesians

---

This [letter] he sent from Rome, as if he had not seen them <note>original: ոպ թէ ոչ էր տեսեալ զնս — a common ancient scholarly debate regarding whether Paul had personally visited the specific recipients of this letter</note>; and the reason for this letter is as follows: The Ephesians were believers in our Lord Jesus Christ, and were intimate with the faith in Him, and held love toward all the saints; and they desired to be established in what is fitting. Having heard [of this] from certain people, the Apostle wrote this letter to them with caution. First, he demonstrates that this mystery should never be considered something new, but rather [existing] from the beginning, before the world was made, according to the will of God; and that Christ suffered for our sake and gave us life. After this, he speaks concerning the calling of the Gentiles <term>Gentiles: հեթանոսաց (het'anosats'), referring to non-Jewish nations</term>, so that he might show them to be worthy of the faith. And he reveals that our calling was not from men, but from the Lord, who is the Son of God; and from this we learn that those who believe in Christ are not man-worshippers, but true God-worshippers. He also indicates himself—that he was sent among these people to preach the Gospel—and that he takes care because of this. Following this, with words of exhortation, he establishes in this letter men and women, fathers and children, masters and servants; and he equips everyone against the Slanderer <note>original: բանսարկուին (bansarkuin) — a title for the Devil, literally "the accuser" or "calumniator"</note> and his demons. He speaks to them again, having well-established and sealed the minds of all against the works of Satan; and thus he completes the letter.

### Chapters of the Epistle to the Ephesians

**1.** Concerning our election in Christ, our new dedication, and perfection.
**2.** A prayer for the knowledge of the goodness of Christ bestowed upon us.
**3.** Concerning the intimacy of the Gentiles and Jews with God through Christ, by hope according to grace.
**4.** Concerning the spreading of His divine wisdom for the enlightenment of the Gentiles and the rebuking of demons.
**5.** A prayer for the Church, for power and for the love of God.
**6.** Instruction on the love of unity, even though the gifts are divided according to various needs.
**7.** Concerning sobriety and righteousness, which makes us into the image of God.
**8.** Concerning a life worthy of holiness, and rebuking evil with deeds—not only with words, but being filled with the Spirit and with psalms, and not with wine.
**9.** A command regarding the household duties of those in authority and those subject to them, according to Christ.
**10.** On the manner of putting on armor <note>original: ՚Ի կերպարանս վառելոյ — literally "in the form of being kindled" or "shining," referring to the Armor of God</note> through the power of Christ.

<sig>AR</sig>

# PROLOGUE
## To the Epistle to the Philippians

He <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul</note> sent this from Rome, because he had seen them and instructed them; and the reasons for this letter are these: The Philippians sent gifts of honor <note>original: "pash-ton-s patuoy" — refers to the financial or material support sent to Paul</note>. Some had come and defiled the minds of the innocent, making excuses regarding the commandments of the Law and <term>circumcision</term> <note>original: "t'lpatut'yun" — a Jewish ritual law that early Christian converts debated</note>; and they were saying, "Without these you cannot be justified." Because of this, the Apostle writes to the Philippians, and first he accepts their labors, and even mentions them by name. After this, he reveals how he gave his defense in Rome; and some were burdened by his bonds <note>Referring to Paul's imprisonment</note>, and were moved with envy. After this, he turned them to love one another; he revealed to them the Savior's love for humanity, that He was God and became man for us. After this, he renders circumcision and the old law as void, explaining that he himself has set aside the reasons for circumcision and says that all this is a loss <note>original: "pakasut'i" — deficiency or disadvantage</note> compared to Christ. Among them, teachers are to be circumcised no more; and he opposes their voice with accusations and says that they are enemies of the cross of Christ. And he accepts the Philippians, for they became partakers in the same. And returning them to their custom, he completes the letter.

---

### Chapters of the Epistle to the Philippians

1. Thanksgiving for the virtue of the Philippians, and prayer for their perfection.
2. An account of his struggling <term>martyrdom</term> <note>original: "nahatakut'yan" — can refer to the struggle of a witness or an athlete, as well as literal death</note> and willingness.
3. Concerning unity and the imitation of life.
4. Concerning Timothy and Epaphroditus <note>Two of Paul’s companions and messengers</note>, whom he sent to them.
5. Concerning spiritual conduct and no longer living according to the flesh, which is the likeness of the death of Christ.
6. Exhortation to certain individuals and to all in common.
7. Acceptance of the ministry <note>original: "spasavorut'ean" — service or material gift</note> that was sent to him.

PAUL AND TIMOTHY, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in the regions of Philippi, along with the <term>bishops</term> <note>original: "episkoposaktsok" — literally "co-bishops" or overseers of the church</note> and <term>deacons</term> <note>original: "sarkavagok" — those appointed to serve the community's needs</note>. <margin>2</margin> ✱ Grace be to you and peace from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>1 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10 11</margin>
✱ I thank my God upon every remembrance of you, ✱ at all times, in all my petitions for you all, offering my prayer with joy ✱ for your fellowship in the Gospel, from the first day until now. ✱ I am confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. ✱ As it seems only right for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart—both in my <term>bonds</term> <note>Referring to Paul's imprisonment in Rome</note> and in my defense and the confirmation of the Gospel—all of you being partakers of my grace. ✱ For God is my witness, how I long for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus. ✱ And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in all wisdom, ✱ so that you may choose what is best, that you may be firm and without offense until the day of Christ, ✱ filled with the fruits of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

**13** So that my **bonds** <note>Paul’s literal chains during his house arrest in Rome</note> in Christ have become manifest in all the <term>palace</term> <note>original: "hraparak"—referring to the Praetorium or the imperial guard's quarters</note> and to everyone else.

**15** Some indeed preach Christ from envy and strife, and some from good will.
**16** The latter do so out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel.
**17** But the former proclaim Christ out of <term>selfish ambition</term> <note>original: "hetsutyun"—contentiousness or partisan spirit</note>, not sincerely, thinking to add affliction to my bonds.
**18** But what of it? In every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and yes, I will continue to rejoice.
**19** For I know that this will result in my <term>salvation</term> <note>In this context, Paul likely means his deliverance from prison or his ultimate vindication</note> through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.
**20** According to my earnest expectation and hope, that I shall be put to shame in nothing, but with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death.
**21** For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
**22** But if I live on in the flesh, this will mean fruit from my labor; and what I shall choose, I do not know.
**23** I am hard-pressed between the two: having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better.
**24** But to remain here in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.
**25** And being confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and joy in the faith.
**26** So that your boasting may abound in Christ Jesus for me by my coming to you again.

<summary>In this passage, Paul reflects on his imprisonment in Rome, noting that it has actually emboldened others to preach the Gospel. He expresses his personal dilemma between the desire to be with Christ after death and the necessity of remaining alive to serve the Philippian church.</summary>

### CHAPTER 3

Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To <margin>1</margin> write the same things to you is not tedious for me, and for you it is very safe. * Watch out for those <term>dogs</term> <note>original: "shants"—a derogatory term Paul uses for false teachers who insisted on Jewish legalism for Gentile converts</note>; <margin>2</margin> watch out for those evil workers; watch out for the <term>mutilation</term> <note>original: "krchatut'e"—a play on words where Paul distinguishes between spiritual circumcision and mere physical cutting</note>. * For we are the <term>circumcision</term> <note>original: "t'lp'atut'iun"—the sign of God's covenant, here applied spiritually</note>, who <margin>3</margin> worship by the Spirit of God, and glory in Christ Jesus, and do not put our confidence in the flesh. * Though I myself <margin>4</margin> have such confidence in the flesh; if anyone else thinks they have reason to be confident in the flesh, I have more: * <term>circumcised</term> on the eighth day, of the <margin>5</margin> nation of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a <term>Pharisee</term> <note>a member of a Jewish sect known for strict adherence to the traditional and written Law</note>; * as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; <margin>6</margin> as to the righteousness that is in the law, I was blameless. * But <margin>7</margin> whatever was gain to me, I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. * More than that, <margin>8</margin> I count all things as loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and I count them as <term>refuse</term> <note>original: "kghkghans"—dung, rubbish, or table scraps; the strongest possible word for worthlessness</note>, that I may gain Christ, * and be found in him, <margin>9</margin> not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God. * To know him and the power <margin>10</margin> of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming like him in his death; * if somehow I may attain to the <margin>11</margin> resurrection from the dead. * Not that I have already obtained this, <margin>12</margin> or have already been made perfect; but I press on to make it my own, because I have been made Christ Jesus' own. * Brothers, I do not consider myself to have <margin>13</margin> attained it; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, * I have my eyes <margin>14</margin>

<meta>This page serves as the introduction and chapter summary for the Epistle to the Colossians, following the conclusion of the Epistle to the Philippians on the previous page. # P R E F A C E
## To the Epistle to the Colossians:

He sends this from Rome, while he had not yet seen them, but had heard of their faith. The occasion for this letter is as follows: The Colossians were considering turning away from the faith in Christ toward the wisdom of the Greeks, and back to legalistic dietary rules and ritual observances <note>original: "nshkharut'is"—referring to remnants of old customs or religious ceremonies.</note>. Having heard all this, the apostle writes this letter to warn them. 

And first, he gives thanks to God, noting that they were delivered from darkness and have come into the true light. He explains that Christ, in whom they have believed, is the image of God and the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "Ban"—the Logos.</note>, through whom all things were made. He shows that it was fitting for Him to act in this way, to be the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead, so that He might lead both and bring life to all. He exhorts them to remain steadfast in the faith and points out that he, Paul, is a servant of the Gospel to which he was called. 

He speaks also concerning the Law, its dietary rules, and the <term>astrological signs</term> <note>original: "astghats'n"—referring to the observation of celestial bodies, seasons, or new moons</note> commanded by it, showing that these old ways have ceased in the presence of the grace of truth. He counsels them not to take pleasure in the "wise men" who, he says, are deceiving you. Furthermore, he provides instruction for parents and children, husbands and wives, servants and masters, disciples, and various others. Having addressed these and other common <term>counsels</term> <note>original: "khorhurdsn"—literally "mysteries" or "deliberations."</note>, he completes the letter, commanding them that when this letter has been read among them, it should also be read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that they themselves should read the letter sent to the Laodiceans.

### Chapters of the Epistle to the Colossians:

1 . Thanksgiving for the Colossians’ reception of grace from God.
2 . A prayer for them, seeking wisdom and a spirit of patient endurance, along with thanksgiving for their reception of <term>adoption</term> <note>original: "ordinut'yan"—the state of being a child of God.</note>.
3 . Concerning Christ’s creation and the renewal that comes through communion with God.
4 . Concerning the conquest of the Gentiles through the flesh and sufferings of Christ, by means of faith.
5 . Concerning his own labors in teaching, which brings this revelation to light.
6 . Concerning being filled with human wisdom <note>likely referring to the proper use of reason</note>, so that through Christ they might possess true wisdom.
7 . That through communion with God, one learns the Law spiritually and lives with Christ.
8 . That fleshly laws require physical examples and not spiritual ones for those who would live by the power of Christ.
9 . Exhortation regarding adoption, modesty, freedom from temptation, love for God, the singing of psalms, and thanksgiving, with praise according to divine conduct.
10 . Regarding being in harmony with one's household. 
2 . [11] Also regarding those who are outsiders.
3 . [12] Regarding prayers and being armed with <term>remedies</term> <note>original: "darmanits'"—meaning cures, provisions, or spiritual care.</note>.

# -> P R E F A C E <-
### -> To the First Epistle to the Thessalonians <-

In this letter, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> writes to everyone, having previously seen them and traveled among them. The reason for this letter is as follows: The Apostle of Christ suffered many afflictions in Beria <note>A city in Macedonia, modern-day Veria</note>, and in Philippi of the Macedonians, and in Corinth. Knowing the situation of the Thessalonians, he feared they might hear he was being tested by the "Tempter" and thus be led into stumbling. Even if some thought they were lost, he first sent Timothy to them, followed by this letter. 

First, he confirms them in the faith so they are never shaken by afflictions, nor deceived by outsiders into Judaism; for they [the Jews] received the "reward" of killing [the Lord], and he speaks of the tribulations the Christians now have. He praises them many times because they kept the teachings just as they received them from him. He writes for the consolation of those who have "fallen asleep" <note>original: 'ննջեցելոցն' (nnjet's'elots'n); a biblical metaphor for those who have died</note> and teaches that they should not be burdened by grief; for death is not destruction, but the path to resurrection. 

Following this, he also teaches regarding the times and seasons, explaining that it is impossible to know this [the exact time of the end]. Instead, let us always be prepared, and let no one think they can learn this through study. Rather, he says, know that the Coming shall be like this: those who remain and are found alive on that day will not precede those who have fallen asleep in the resurrection; instead, there will be a transformation for everyone together. He teaches further and provides an example for them to exceed their usual habits, to be joyful in hope, and to pray and give thanks to the Lord for one another. He adjures them to read this letter to all the brothers, and thus he completes the letter.

### Chapters of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians

**1.** Praise for the Thessalonians regarding the worthy struggles of the apostles.

**2.** His longing and joy over them, and concerns regarding how they might be made perfect.

**3.** Prayer to God and Christ for His coming to them, and for the growth and strengthening of the Thessalonians until the coming of Christ.

**4.** Instruction on sobriety and righteousness in the choice of brotherly love, and for each person to tend to their own work.

**5.** Teaching on the undoing of death for both the living and the dead at the manifestation of Christ.

**6.** Concerning the sudden coming of Christ; how it is necessary to be found prepared with diligence, faith, hope, love, honor, peace, patience, and love for God.

**7.** Prayer for the holiness of the spirit, breath, and body.

# PREFACE
## To the Second Letter to the Thessalonians.

He sent this from Rome <note>While the text states Rome, most modern biblical scholars believe 2 Thessalonians was written from Corinth shortly after the first letter.</note>, and the reason for this letter is as follows: 
Some among the Thessalonians were living idly and without discipline, taking advantage of the brothers, and they were unstable regarding the coming of the Lord. When the Apostle heard all of this—both what was told to him and what he perceived through the Spirit—he wrote this letter. First, he acknowledges their faith to comfort them, and he boasts of them amidst the tribulations he was suffering for Christ's sake. He comforts them by speaking of God’s justice upon those who were acting unrighteously toward them. After this, he teaches regarding the coming of the Savior, warning that no one should deceive them, whether by word, by spirit, or by a letter [purporting to be] from him, so as not to trouble or alienate them. For [he explains] the great rebellion <note>Armenian: ապստամբութի խառնակ (apstambut'i kharnak); literally a "confused" or "tumultuous rebellion," referring to the Great Apostasy.</note> must come first, followed by the Antichrist <note>Armenian: հակառակքրիստոսն (hakarak-k'ristosn); literally "the one who is against Christ."</note>, the son of perdition, who comes with false arts and signs through the cooperation of Satan to perform wonders. After this, he urges them to be strong and to hold fast to the traditions they were taught by him. He commands them to no longer have fellowship with the undisciplined, but to reject those who are not engaged in honest work <note>Armenian: գործս խաբէութե (gorts khabeut'e); likely referring to those living by deception or avoiding labor.</note>. He commanded them and everyone else not to listen to their words, but to gather against such behavior, and having prayed in peace, he completed the letter. He wrote the greeting with his own hand, which he commands as a sign in all his letters.

# PREFACE
## To the Epistle to the Hebrews.

This was sent from Italy; and the reason for this Epistle is as follows:
❦ Because those who were Jews stood firmly by the law and the commandments, for this reason the apostle Paul—who became the teacher of the Gentiles and was sent to the Gentiles to preach the gospel—wrote to all the Gentiles. He also wrote to those of the circumcision <note>original: "թլփատութենէն" (t'lpatut'enen); referring to Jewish converts to Christianity.</note> among the believing Hebrews a letter of instruction concerning the coming of Christ <note>original: "Քի" (K'i), abbreviation for Christ.</note> and concerning the cessation of the shadowy laws <note>This refers to the idea that the Old Testament laws were "shadows" or precursors to the "reality" found in Christ.</note>. And first, he points to the prophets regarding these matters, because they heralded the gospel of the Savior, and he followed after them. He calls the prophets "servants" and messengers of His coming; but the same Christ he calls the "Son of God" <note>original: "որդի այ" (ordi ay), where "ay" is an abbreviation for "Astuco" (of God).</note>, through whom all things were made. And he shows that this Son became man, who, having been offered as a sacrifice in his own body, purified death—not by the blood of bulls and goats, but by the blood of Christ came the salvation of mankind. He also shows this: that the law made no one perfect, but rather held the promise of future goods, and did not provide rest for the people; instead, he makes us all partakers in the day of rest. Again, he shows that the sacrifice of the high priesthood proceeded from Aaron until Christ, whose type <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future one.</note> is Melchizedek, and not from the line of Levi. He signifies the righteousness of our fathers through faith, and not by the works of the law; and again he turns them back to the customary way, accepting their endurance for the sake of Christ, and concludes the Epistle by honoring the elders.

## Chapters of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Regarding this Epistle to the Hebrews, some say that it might not be by Paul because of its style <note>original: "նկարագրին" (nkaragrin); literally "description" or "image," here referring to the literary character or prose style.</note>, and because he did not place his name at the beginning as he did in his other Epistles, and because of the saying: "How shall we escape if we neglect such a salvation, which began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed to us by those who heard Him, with God bearing witness through signs and wonders?" <note>This is a paraphrase of Hebrews 2:3–4.</note> There are reasons for the change in the style of this Epistle: namely, that it was written to the Hebrews in their own language, and they say it was later translated—some say by Luke, and others by Clement <note>referring to Clement of Rome.</note>, whose style it indeed carries. But as for not writing his name in the Epistle here, the reasons are fitting: Paul was the apostle to the Gentiles and not to the Jews; for an agreement had been given by the Lord to Peter and the other apostles that he [Paul], along with Barnabas, would go to the Gentiles, and Peter’s group to the circumcision. And now, since the preaching was by agreement, and those of the Jews were hesitant—as if Paul were teaching some kind of rebellion—he rightly gives this Epistle to the Hebrews to be recognized for the sake of unity; and in writing to them, it was not the custom to set his name at the head of the Epistle. But the Epistle further testifies in the following parts...

<meta>This page continues the introductory material for the Epistle to the Hebrews. It concludes the opening remarks on the context of the letter and provides a numbered thematic summary (an ancient "table of contents") of the major arguments and sections of the Epistle.</meta>

Where it is appropriate, writing that "women also were sharers in my sorrows" <note>This likely refers to the "partners in suffering" mentioned in Hebrews 10:34 or the greeting to the sisters in faith in chapter 13.</note> and saying, "pray even more that I may be quickly restored to you" <note>original: "վաղվաղակի պատսպարեցայց ձեզ" (vaghvaghaki patsparyetsayts dzez); referencing Hebrews 13:19.</note>. And there are many other things that show us the sacred letters, as the reading itself, moving forward, teaches:

1. The divine discourse concerning Christ <note>original: "Ածխօսութի քի" (Atskhosut'i K'i); Theology of Christ.</note>: His glory with the Father and his authority over all, together with the holiness he performed on earth, from which he was raised back to heavenly glory.
2. That the glory of Christ is not by necessity <note>meaning: not coerced or purely human necessity.</note>, but divine and creative; for which reason it is not here in this world, where things are of necessity, but in the world to come.
3. That he took flesh according to providence, to be a partaker in suffering and to be in kinship with us, for the salvation of mankind, reconciling us to himself through his death.
4. That it is right to believe in Christ just as they believed in Moses; but to a greater degree, as one believes in God rather than man. 
  a. In which one must fear the former exile.
5. Foresight by example: to hasten beforehand toward the foretold rest.
6. The fear of judgment and the sweetness of grace according to the priesthood, by which he shared in our human suffering.
7. A reprimand for those who are lacking in the newly-given teaching. 
  a. Encouragement toward growth, as if there were no "second beginning" <note>Refers to the idea of not needing to lay the foundations of faith again.</note>. 
  b. Consolation together with thanksgiving.
8. That the promises <note>original: "աւետիքն" (avetik'n); literally "good news" or "glad tidings."</note> of God are firm, and the same are confirmed with oaths.
9. Concerning Melchizedek, who served as a type of Christ in name, in judgment, in life, in death, and in priesthood. 
  a. In which he was more highly honored than Abraham.
10. That the priesthood of Aaron is to cease, because it was earthly; and the heavenly priesthood, which belongs to Christ, is to be established from another tribe, not according to the flesh, nor according to carnal law.
11. The superiority of the second covenant over the first in glory and holiness.
12. Concerning the blood of Christ by which the new covenant is established; for this is true holiness in eternal things, and not with the blood of animals which were offered many times.
13. Testimonies regarding holiness alone, and submission to God. 
  a. Encouragement to prepare the way according to faith.
14. An urging to haste because of the fear of the approaching judgment.
15. Concerning bringing a good beginning to a good completion.
16. Concerning faith, which made the ancients glorious.
17. Concerning patience, to run the course with Christ.
18. Concerning sobriety <note>original: "զգաստութ" (zgastut'); also meaning discipline or alertness.</note> until the time of the Coming, lest we miss the mark like Esau, who found no place for repentance.
19. That the things to come are more terrifying than those under Moses, and worthy of much haste now.
20. Concerning brotherly love and hospitality toward strangers. 
  a. Concerning sobriety. 
  b. Concerning contentment. 
  c. Concerning imitating the fathers.
21. Not to remain living carnally according to the law, but spiritually according to the virtue of Christ.
22. Prayer to God for progress in virtue and for thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER 1

1 **IN MANY PORTIONS, AND IN** many ways, God spoke of old to our fathers through the prophets. 
2 * In these last days, He has spoken to us through His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, through whom He also created the ages <note>original: "զյաւիտեանսն" (z-yaviteansn); this term can refer to both time/eternity and the physical worlds or universes.</note>.
3 * Who is the light of His glory and the very image of His essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature or being of God</term>, who bears all things by the word of His power. Having accomplished the cleansing of our sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.
4 * Having become so much greater than the angels, as the name He inherited is more excellent than theirs.
5 * For to which of the angels did He ever say: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you"? And again: "I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son"?
6 * But when He again brings the firstborn into the world, He says: "Let all the angels of God worship him."
7 * But regarding the angels He says: "Who made His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire."
8 * But to the Son He says: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom."
9 * You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness more than your companions.
10 * And: "You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands."
11 * They shall perish, but you remain and endure; they shall all wear out like a garment,
12 * And like a cloak, you will roll them up <note>The text breaks here mid-sentence, following the original manuscript's page ending.</note>.

---

<margin>'In the titles' some read: The Epistle to the Hebrews.</margin>

<term>High Priest (քահանայապետ)</term>: The supreme religious leader; here, Christ is described as the ultimate High Priest.
<term>Sacrifices (պատարագս)</term>: Offerings or liturgies performed for the atonement of sins.
<term>Melchizedek (մելքիսեդեկի)</term>: A mysterious king and priest from the Old Testament (Genesis) who serves as a prototype for Christ’s eternal priesthood.
<term>Milk (կաթին)</term>: A metaphor for basic, elementary Christian teachings, contrasted with "solid food" for the mature.

The author concludes by rebuking the readers for their lack of spiritual maturity, comparing their need for basic instruction to a need for milk rather than solid food.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Epistle to the Hebrews, picking up in the middle of Chapter 6. The previous page discussed the danger of falling away from faith and the need for spiritual maturity. This page transitions from God’s certain promise to Abraham to the introduction of the mysterious figure Melchizedek.</meta>

<header>EPISTLE</header>

<margin>13</margin> through patience <note>original: "մտութբ," abbreviation for "համբերութեամբ"</note> they inherited the promises. ✱ For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by,
<margin>14</margin> ✱ he swore by himself, and said: "Yes, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you."
<margin>15</margin> ✱ And so, having been patient, he reached the promise.
<margin>16</margin> ✱ For indeed, humans swear by what is higher than themselves; and for every dispute, the oath is the final word for confirmation.
<margin>17</margin> ✱ In this way, God, wanting even more to show the heirs of the promise the unchangeable nature of his counsel, mediated with an oath.
<margin>18</margin> ✱ So that by two unchangeable things—in which it is impossible for God to lie—we who have taken refuge might have strong encouragement <note>original: "մխիթարութի" (mkhitarutiun) – comfort or consolation</note> to seize the hope set before us.
<margin>19</margin> ✱ This hope we have as an anchor for our souls, firm and secure, which enters into the inner side of the curtain <note>The "curtain" or veil refers to the partition in the Temple that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, where God’s presence dwelt</note>,
<margin>20</margin> ✱ where Jesus, our forerunner, entered on our behalf, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

### CHAPTER 7

<margin>1</margin> For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, met Abraham as he was returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him.
<margin>2</margin> ✱ To him Abraham also gave a tenth of everything. First, <term>Melchizedek</term> is translated as "king of righteousness," and then "king of Salem," which means "king of peace."
<margin>3</margin> ✱ Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.

# P R E F A C E
## To the First Epistle to Timothy

<image-desc>Decorative banner with abstract scrollwork patterns spanning the width of the page.</image-desc>

This was sent from Macedonia, and the reason for this letter is this: 
In Ephesus, some among the Jews were wandering about; and having begun with <term>strange teachings<note>original: "օտար վարդապետութբն" (otar vardapetutyan) — Referring to heterodox or non-apostolic doctrines that deviated from the established gospel.</note></term>, they opposed the truth by alleging various defilements. Upon hearing this, the Apostle sent Timothy to remain there in order to correct them. He also wrote this letter, commanding Timothy beforehand to understand the <term>ministry<note>original: "դեւատարս" (devatars) — This word is likely an OCR error or a variant for "դաւանութիւնս" (confessions/doctrines) or "դաստիարակութիւնս" (instructions); it literally translates to "carried by demons," which does not fit the context of Paul's instructions to Timothy.</note></term> of Christ. He instructs him also regarding the laws, in order to restrain those who were speaking outside of the <term>upright teaching<note>original: "ուղիղ վարդապետութբն" (ughigh vardapetutyan) — Equivalent to "orthodoxy" or sound doctrine.</note></term>. He rebukes even those men themselves, Hymenaeus and Alexander, who suffered shipwreck in their faith, whom he delivered to Satan so that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme. Having commanded these things and established them, he sets down <term>ecclesiastical canons<note>original: "կանոն եկեղեցական" (kanon ekeghetsakan) — Early church rules governing behavior and organization.</note></term> regarding prayers: namely, how or where or for whom one should pray. He instructs women to learn in silence, especially in the church, and not to teach. He writes concerning <term>bishops<note>original: "եպիսկոպոսաց" (yepiskoposats)</note></term>, priests, and deacons—how they should conduct themselves and what sort of people they should be. He also discusses those under the care of the church, such as the age at which a woman ought to be formally called a widow, and those who are called so but do not take care. He advises the young widows to marry and not to live in impurity. He also commands the rich not to be arrogant and not to hope in riches. After this, he speaks of the teachers who labor; he warns Timothy to know the teaching and the time in which some will turn away from the faith. He instructs them also regarding the holiness of foods and commands them to avoid those who were wanderers, through whom some became transgressors of the faith. Thus the letter is completed.

### Chapters of the First Epistle to Timothy:

1. Concerning love toward God as leadership, which makes one free from divine necessity. 2. Concerning his own choice as an <term>evangelist<note>original: "աւետարանիչ" (avetaranich)</note></term>, changing from a persecutor by the grace of Christ.

3. A commandment regarding faith and single-minded service, without which one would remain in a state of destitute distress.

4. Concerning prayers for everyone, and in every place with innocence, without disturbance, and with modesty.

5. Concerning how it is lawful for men to be teachers, and not women, because of nature and because of the pains that entered through deception, which the birth of Christ resolves, along with their faith and conduct.

6. Concerning the primacy of the bishop. 7. In which he speaks of deacons, both men and women. 8. Concerning the <term>Divine Incarnation<note>original: "ածեղէն մարմնանալոյն" (atseghen marmnanaloyn) — Refers to the mystery of God becoming human in Jesus Christ.</note></term>. 9. In which he speaks of demonic heresies that are to come.

10. Concerning the battle for godliness with hope.

10. <note>The list repeats the number 10 (ժ) in the original text.</note> Concerning the care of oneself and the church.

10. <note>The list repeats the number 10 (ժ) a third time.</note> Concerning the propriety of approaching each person.

### CHAPTER 1

<margin>ak</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'P' within an ornate square frame featuring floral motifs.</image-desc>PAUL, AN APOSTLE of Jesus Christ, by the command of God our Savior, and Jesus Christ our hope; * to Timothy, my beloved son in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>1</margin> * As I urged you to remain in Ephesus, while I was going to Macedonia, so that you might command certain ones not to teach <term>foreign doctrines<note>original: "օտարուսմունս" (otarusmuns) — teachings that deviate from the apostolic tradition, often referring to early Gnostic or divergent Jewish-Christian ideas.</note></term>, * and not to attend to fables and endless <term>genealogies<note>original: "տոհմաթիւս" (tohmatiws) — lineage lists which were often used in the ancient world to claim spiritual or social authority.</note></term>; which rather stir up questions, and not the divine stewardship in faith. * For the goal of the command is love, from a pure heart, and from a good conscience, and from unfeigned faith; * from which some have strayed, turning aside to empty chatter; * wishing to be teachers of the law, while they themselves do not understand what they are saying, nor concerning what they are so insistent. * We know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully; * but let this be known: that the law is not for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who dishonor fathers and mothers...

<meta>This page serves as the introduction and table of contents for the Second Epistle of Paul to Timothy. It follows the conclusion of the First Epistle, providing historical context for Paul’s second imprisonment in Rome and summarizing the key themes of the letter.</meta>

<image-desc>Decorative horizontal band at the top with a repeating circular pattern.</image-desc>

# P R E F A C E

->To the Second Epistle to Timothy.<-

This letter he sends again from Rome; and this is the reason for this letter: Those who were companions of Paul abandoned him. The Apostle intended for Timothy to come to him, writing this letter, and he notes the memory of Timothy's piety and the faith of his ancestors. After that, he recounts that those in Asia—Phygellus and Hermogenes—turned away from him. Having seen his chains upon arriving in Rome, Onesiphorus <note>A Christian from Ephesus who sought out Paul in his Roman prison (2 Timothy 1:16).</note> welcomed him and remained with him. He commands him [Timothy] to take up sufferings. He also mentions Hymenaeus and Philetus, who raised a disturbance; for they were put to shame and found to be transgressors, saying that the resurrection of the dead has already occurred, and they turned some away. Especially regarding the strife among them, he warns him against their teaching. He announces that a time will come in which people will be self-loving, slanderers, and unbridled; when you see all this, warn the congregations so they do not fall into these habits; for they turn the gentle toward straying doctrines. And he indicates the time of his own coming [end]; and he hastens and bears witness, commanding him to come to him quickly; commanding him to bring the cloak <note>original: "փիլոնն" (p’ilonn) — the heavy traveling cloak Paul left at Troas (2 Timothy 4:13).</note> and the books. He warns him to be on guard against Alexander the coppersmith, for he showed him much evil; and thus he completes the letter.

### Chapters for the Second Epistle to Timothy.

**1.** Praise for Timothy’s faith, and encouragement toward patience through worthy grace.
**2.** Wherein he himself says to be enduring when he suffers.
**3.** Concerning the proper administration of divine religion.
**4.** Concerning being free from worldly care through virtue, having food without labor <note>This likely refers to spiritual sustenance or the support provided to those dedicated to the ministry.</note>.
**5.** Concerning faith in Christ and specific patience according to worthy honor.
**6.** Concerning correct doctrine, and holy and peaceful conduct, and against opponents.
**7.** A prediction concerning the increase of evil people and the rebuking of deception.
**8.** Encouragement for him to be an imitator [of Paul] in obedience to God, contrary to the senseless, and concerning those whom he commands Timothy to stand against.
**9.** Concerning his own approaching end <note>original: "վախճանին" (vakhchanin) — meaning end, decease, or the completion of a journey.</note> in eternal glory.

# P R E F A C E
## To the Epistle to Titus

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut horizontal divider featuring repeating scroll and floral patterns sits above the main title.</image-desc>

He sent this from Nicopolis <note>A city in Greece where Paul intended to winter; see Titus 3:12.</note>, for he spent the winter there. The reason for this letter is as follows: he left Titus in Crete <note>A large island in the Mediterranean.</note> so that he might establish administrators <term>ministers/elders</term> in every city. Many who were there had begun to make excuses regarding the Law <note>Referring to the Mosaic Law and the "Judaizers" who insisted on its observance for Christians.</note>, whereby they stood against the assembly. From here Paul also writes; and first, he gives thanks to God for his [Titus's] godliness. He also indicates the faith which they have in Christ: not to be like children, but to be fully prepared and cautious. He commands, according to God’s covenant, to establish administrators, and to teach them what sort of people they should be. He urges them to correct those who were contrary to the sound faith—especially those of the circumcision <note>Jewish converts who insisted on the necessity of circumcision.</note>. He sees that the Cretans were idle, and it is fitting to urge them [to work]. He teaches them that all food is clean to the clean. He describes how responses should be given, so that they may wisely and becomingly instruct the young women. He defines how servants <note>original: ծառայքն (tsarayk'n) - meaning servants or bondservants.</note> should be faithful to their own masters. And at the end, he reminds them that the Savior’s grace did not justify us by works, but according to His own love for humanity <note>original: մարդասիրութեն (mardasirut‘en) - a common Armenian theological term for God's philanthropy or love for mankind.</note>. He commands them to avoid legalistic instruction, describing such things as corruptible. And when he sends Artemas to him, he gives instructions; and he desires that they learn by experience to persevere in good works. And thus he concludes the letter.

## Chapters of the Epistle to Titus

A. On ministers useful for service and the rebuking of unbelievers.
B. Against those who preside with physical purity [alone], and regarding spiritual virtue.
C. Instructions which must be given according to each age group.
D. On servants, that they too may serve worthily of Christ’s grace.
E. On rulers, regarding worthy obedience according to the meekness of Christ.
F. Instruction to turn away from heretical questioners <note>original: հերձուածողական քննողացն (herdzuatsoghakan knnoghatsn) - those who examine or debate in a way that causes schism or heresy.</note>.

# PREFACE
## To the Epistle to Philemon.

This letter was sent from Rome on account of Onesimus. This Onesimus, a servant of Philemon, fled and came to the Apostle. Having been trained by him, he became noble in service. For this reason, [Paul] writes to Philemon concerning him, entrusting Onesimus to him so that he might be moved to receive him with acceptance—not as a slave, but as a brother. He goes on to call Philemon’s house a place of hospitality for strangers, asking that he prepare a lodging for him upon his arrival. Thus he concludes the letter.

### Chapters of the Epistle to Philemon.

1. Praise of Philemon and thanksgiving for him.
2. The recommendation of Onesimus, the runaway slave, and the plea for his salvation from his former low status.

---

(9) Some [manuscripts]: reject contentions... they are unprofitable and vain.
(10) One example: After the first, [second,] and third admonition, reject him.
(11) Some: Self-condemned. (12) Some: Artemon or Tychicus... in Nicopolis. (13) Some: That they may lack nothing. (15) One example, following Voskan <note>referring to the 1666 Voskan Yerevantsi Bible</note>, adds: Grace be with you all, Amen.

# TO PHILEMON,
## AND TO ARCHIPPUS THE DEACON,
### AND TO APPHIA.

---

<margin>1</margin> **PAUL, A PRISONER OF JE**sus Christ, and Timothy our brother: To Philemon our beloved and fellow worker, * and to Apphia our sister <note>original: քեռ (k'er); literally "sister." In early Christian usage, this referred to a female member of the faith community.</note>, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house. * Grace to you and peace from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

* I thank my God at all times, making mention of you in my prayers, * as I hear of your faith and the love which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints. * So that the <term>fellowship of your faith</term> <note>original: հաղորդութիւն հաւատոց (haghortut'yun havatots); refers to the shared participation or communion of believers in their common faith.</note> may become effective through the knowledge of every good thing that is in you in Christ Jesus. * For I have received great joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you, brother.

<margin>2</margin> * Therefore, though I have much boldness in Christ to command you what is fitting, * yet for love’s sake, I rather appeal to you—being such a person as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. * I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in my chains, <term>Onesimus</term> <note>The name Onesimus (Ոնեսիմոս) means "useful" or "profitable" in Greek. Paul uses this meaning as a play on words in the following verse.</note>, * who formerly was useless to you, but now is useful to both you and me. * I have sent him back to you; and you, receive him—that is, <term>my own heart</term> <note>original: զիմ աղիս (zim aghis); literally "my bowels" or "my viscera." In ancient thought, the internal organs were considered the seat of deep emotion and affection.</note>. * Whom I wished to keep with me, so that on your behalf he might serve me in the chains of the gospel. * But without your consent I did not want to do anything, so that your good deed might not be by necessity...

* *According to the proper conclusion of this letter, in the older manuscripts there are other fragmentary sayings, perhaps from Josephus... <note>The text here mentions "Յսաֆայ" (Yusafay), likely a reference to the historian Josephus or a scribal name associated with a specific tradition.</note> among which is this: "These books were copied from the Caesarean copies, which are kept in the east among the books of Saint Pamphilus, written by his own hand."* <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD) was a famous scholar and martyr whose library was a primary source for early biblical manuscripts.</note>

<meta>This page marks the transition from the Pauline Epistles (ending with Philemon) to the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse). It provides a traditional Armenian preface that summarizes the theological purpose and the symbolic content of the vision of St. John.</meta>

# P R E F A C E
## To the Revelation of John.

This book of the holy Evangelist John is called "Revelation," in which first the prophetic spirit [reveals] the things to come from the crucifixion of Christ until the end. It is called "Revelation" because certain aspects of future events are made more accurately known here than in other books. The reason for this Revelation is as follows: because before communicating openly with others, God the Father gave this firm and useful [revelation] to the world. For this reason, the prophets—who were patriarchs—first foretold the divine dispensation <note>original: տնօրէնութիւն (tnorēnut'iwn); a technical theological term referring to God’s plan or "economy" for the salvation of humanity through the incarnation of Christ.</note> of Christ as the foundation of godliness. The Apostles then preached the same: that it was God who became man and was crucified. Once the churches were established in this firm faith, then the tribulations that were to come thereafter—especially in the days of the Antichrist <note>original: նեռն (neṛn); the Armenian term for the Antichrist, likely derived from the Greek "neron" (Nero), who was historically associated with the figure.</note>—were foretold through this Revelation to prepare for the truth of the events in their time. 

Among the things said here, those which occur before the Antichrist and those during his time are partly mentioned in the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostolic teachings. However, some things are found only in this book, such as the sign of the name of the Antichrist which he stamps upon the foreheads of the lost; the testimony and death of Enoch and Elijah; the binding and releasing of Satan; the sea of glass; the New Jerusalem; and the various plagues contained in this book. According to the law of prophecy, [the author] sees future events through physical imagery—those marked for death according to the mystery—golden lampstands, the awesome figure of a man, thrones, visions of precious stones, types of plagues, and such, one by one. 

First, [he describes] the glorified churches remaining in virtue and growth, and those who have fallen away returning to the same. By the opening of the seals of the book in chronological order, he reveals what has occurred, from the preaching of the Apostles to the severe persecutions, wherein the innocent <note>original: անձօժիքն (andzōzhik’n); referring to those who are pure or without guilt.</note> shine more brightly and the brave who rejoice are honored. Then follow the inquiries <note>possibly referring to the trumpet judgments or woes</note> that occur before the end, including the retribution upon the vengeful, during which the saints praise God. He turns also to the image of the woman who was in labor to give birth, revealing the war of the dragon against the Church from the beginning of the Gospel onward, until the seven-headed dragon, which is the Antichrist. He speaks of the various ministries of the angels until the Antichrist is cast into Gehenna. He returns to speak of the binding of Satan by the Cross, his release at the coming of the Antichrist, and his being cast again into a sea of fire and sulfur. Finally, he speaks of the general resurrection and judgment, and of the new heaven and earth which the righteous shall inherit.

2. That...

* At the conclusion of the Book of Revelation, many add the "Rest of John the Evangelist" <note>An apocryphal account of the Apostle John's passing</note>; which our copies have omitted, instead placing the colophon of Nerses of Lambron <note>A 12th-century Armenian Archbishop of Tarsus known for his translations and ecumenical work.</note>. In which, having shown through the testimony of the Church Fathers that this book was accepted by the Church in the rank of the divine New Testament scriptures, he adds: "Being a fellow-traveler with them, we have handed this down to the children of the holy Church within the arrangement of the apostolic books, as it is truly an apostolic revelation; and a true account of Ararat <note>Likely referring to the Armenian homeland or the 'lofty' nature of the text</note> re-edited from the Greek and through the humble translation of Nerses, along with a careful examination of its various copies, it was brought into the Armenian Church." <meta>This page transitions from the formal conclusion of the New Testament to an editorial appendix. It lists additional apocryphal or supplementary books included in this edition based on various manuscripts, following the catchword "բոյն" from the previous gathering.</meta>

# APPENDIX
## OF THIS DIVINELY-BREATHED BOOK <note>original: "Astvatsashunch" — the standard Armenian term for the Bible, meaning "God-breathed."</note>

---

->N O T I C E<-

According to our promise made in the preface and throughout the notes, we have deemed it appropriate here at the conclusion to summarize separately not only those writings of the same kind found in the order of the model <note>The editor is referring to the primary manuscript or "exemplar" used for this edition.</note> we set before us—which we have indicated in their respective places—but also whatever we found in other copies related to the same purpose. For this reason, we rightfully give the first place among these to the Book of Sirach <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach.</note>; which three modern copies contained within the contents of the volume, placed after the Book of Wisdom, and which also appeared in a few individual manuscripts, as we have shown in the preface.

Second, we have arranged the third book of Ezra, which according to the Latin tradition is considered Fourth Ezra <note>The numbering of the Books of Ezra/Esdras varies significantly between the Armenian, Greek, and Latin Bibles. What Armenians call 3 Ezra is often 4 Ezra in the Latin Vulgate.</note>; which was also contained in three modern copies—namely, the fourth, fifth, and seventh manuscripts—written after the three books of Ezra. However, these were without a preface or a list of chapters; by which, and by other circumstances of the style of composition, it was clearly evident that it was translated and introduced into the canon of the books at a later time. But from which original text, when, or by whose hand this was done, we cannot say with certainty. For when we wished to compare this version with the Latin one translated by <term>Voskan <note>Voskan Yerevantsi (1614–1674), the bishop who printed the first Armenian Bible in Amsterdam in 1666. He famously adapted some parts of the Armenian text to match the Latin Vulgate.</note></term>, we saw such variation between them that in many places there is no comparison at all. Nevertheless, we have tried as much as possible to indicate the correspondence of the chapters and words of the Latin alongside it, a task which two of the aforementioned copies had begun but left incomplete.

Third, it was perhaps not inappropriate to provide in this appendix...

<summary>This page serves as an editorial introduction to the Appendix of the Armenian Bible, explaining the inclusion of the Book of Sirach and the Book of Ezra (4 Ezra). The editor notes the textual discrepancies between Armenian manuscripts and the 1666 printing by Voskan Yerevantsi.</summary>

<keywords>Appendix, Book of Sirach, Ezra, Esdras, Voskan Yerevantsi, Armenian Bible, manuscript comparison, canon, translation style</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the list of editorial additions and justifications for including specific apocryphal texts in this edition of the Armenian Bible. of the text, and to place the blessings <note>These are the Old Testament canticles or hymns, such as the Song of Moses, usually appended to the Psalter.</note> of the Psalter which our manuscript exemplar contained, attached to the end of each canon of the psalms, as we have announced there. However, the proper proportion of this volume restrains us from adding such a repetition of words, especially given the harsh differences found among them. And since the Prayer of Manasseh the King was also among their number, we have selected and arranged that as well, as it was missing from other manuscript copies of this book.

**Fourth** addition: we deemed it appropriate to include the Letter of the Corinthians to Paul the Apostle, together with the apostle's response <note>This refers to the apocryphal "Third Epistle to the Corinthians," which was historically part of the Armenian New Testament canon.</note>. For these letters were found in almost every manuscript copy of this volume—in many, as in ours, at the end of the fourteen epistles of Paul, and in some, placed within them after the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. For this reason, perhaps, some took the liberty to introduce these two letters into the order of the Lectionary <note>original: "Chashots" — the liturgical book containing the scripture readings for the Eucharist.</note> readings after the week of the Fast of the Catechumens <note>original: "Arachavorats" — a unique Armenian fast occurring ten weeks before Easter.</note>, on the days of the Epistle of Peter, as is seen in the Lectionary written at Holy Etchmiadzin, as well as in some other recent copies. 

Although European writers remained ignorant of the Greek original and these letters remained unknown to them for many centuries, the Englishman Whiston <note>William Whiston (1667–1752), an English theologian and mathematician.</note> was the first to judge them there. Having come across an incomplete copy in Utrecht, he published a translation from the Armenian language into Latin in the year 1715. Regarding this, the idle opinions of La Croze <note>Maturin Veyssière de La Croze, a French scholar who suggested the letters were Armenian forgeries.</note>—claiming that they were something invented by the Armenians—can be seen in Fabricius’s *Faith: On the Unknown Books of the New Testament* <note>original: "Havatk anyayt grots nor ktak" — referring to Johann Albert Fabricius's *Codex Apocryphus Novi Testamenti*.</note>. But after that, the two Whiston brothers in England translated them again from a more complete copy into two languages—that is, into Greek and Latin—alongside the Armenian original. Appending them to the history of Khorenatsi <note>The *History of Armenia* by Moses of Khoren.</note>, they printed them in London in the year 1736, though even in that edition errors are not lacking.

**Fifth**, we have arranged the "Rest of John the Apostle" <note>original: "Hangistn Hovhannu" — also known as the "Death" or "Assumption" of John, an apocryphal account of the apostle's departure from life.</note>; this is the final word of his testament. In many copies besides our own, it was attached after the Book of Revelation. This writing was so well known and esteemed among our people from the very beginning that it was not only included in the readings of the Lectionary and the Ritual Book <note>original: "Mashtots" — the book of liturgical offices and sacraments.</note>, but was also cited as a faithful message in testimony of his divine words by the Doctors of the Church <note>original: "Vardapets" — the learned celibate priests and theologians of the Armenian tradition.</note>, and was commented upon in detail...
